articles.title: To Secure Arctic, NORTHCOM Builds Closer Ties to Pacific, European Commands
articles.body:
U.S. Airmen assigned to the 115th Fighter Wing, Wisconsin Air National Guard, marshal an F-35A Lightning II aircraft at Pituffik Space Base, Greenland, Sept. 10, 2026. U.S. Air National Guard photo by Master Sgt. Mary Greenwood
Audio of this article is brought to you by the Air & Space Forces Association, honoring and supporting our Airmen, Guardians, and their families. Find out more at afa.org
U.S. Northern Command plans to sign an agreement with its European and Pacific counterparts to enhance coordination and close security seams in the Arctic, a strategically vital region where all three commands converge, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine.
NORTHCOM’s Gen. Gregory M. Guillot, U.S. European Command’s Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, and U.S. Pacific Command’s Adm. Samuel Paparo will finalize the agreement, which aims to strengthen information sharing and ensure that adversaries cannot exploit the geographic boundaries among the commands.
U.S. Northern Command’s long-standing motto, “We have the watch,” has taken on greater urgency in recent years as the potential means to attack the U.S. Arctic region have grown. Today, the command’s geographic focus stretches across Canada, Greenland, and south to Mexico and parts of the Caribbean, and the potential dangers have expanded to include a range of emerging threats, from intelligence-gathering balloons to ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones.
Guillot, in a September interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, said the command has managed the growth well. “Over the last couple of years, we’ve received a few new missions with Greenland, the Southern Border, Golden Dome, and the counter-UAS mission, and we’ve been able to evolve and incorporate those into our daily homeland defense operations, I think, seamlessly,” said Guillot, whose responsibilities also include heading the binational U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command, known as NORAD.
“The command is growing as the number of threats and the number of avenues of approach that they can use to threaten us increase,” he added of NORTHCOM.
The Arctic’s strategic importance has grown as melting polar ice has opened up the region for greater commercial traffic and resource exploitation.
Russia, which owns more than half the Arctic coastline, has long projected its military might in the region.
More recently, China has sought to assert itself as an Arctic nation, not because it controls territory there but because of its value as a transit venue, shortening the trade routes between China and Europe. China operates research vessels there, including submersibles.
“They’re seeking to move themselves forward militarily and become global power projectors, not regional power projectors, and part of that will involve holding us at risk through the Arctic and ensuring that policy in the Arctic reflects their interests,” retired Gen. Glen D. VanHerck, Guillot’s predecessor at NORTHCOM and NORAD, said in an interview.
A joint China-Russia bomber patrol in the region, which took off in 2024 from a Russian base, demonstrated closer ties between the two and raised concerns across North America and Europe about their growing cooperation.
“When you see Russia and China cooperating militarily in the Arctic, with a greater capacity arguably than anywhere else on Earth, I think that should give some signals that we should be paying attention to what’s going on in the region,” said Iris Ferguson, who served as deputy assistant secretary of defense for Arctic and global resilience from 2022-2025.
Ferguson sees closing the gaps between U.S. military commands that converge in the Arctic region as essential to enhanced security.
“There are multiple seams in the Arctic for the United States,” she said. “The one between NORTHCOM and EUCOM is a significant one and is one area that deserves more attention.”
NORTHCOM led the drive to formalize an agreement with its fellow combatant commands, working closely with EUCOM and its boss, Grynkewich, who is also NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, with critical ties to NATO’s Nordic allies. Through NATO, Grynkewich is responsible for defending what NATO dubs the High North, comprising Canada, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, and the U.S. The alliance held multiple large-scale Arctic exercises this past summer, some of which Air & Space Forces Magazine experienced firsthand. NATO’s Arctic Sentry “enhanced vigilance activity” operates in cooperation with NORAD and NORTHCOM, and alliance officials describe that cooperation as at a level not seen in decades.
Guillot said the potential threats aren’t limited to America’s largest potential adversaries.
“I see the threat to our continent changing not just from Russia and China, but from multiple adversaries,” Guillot said. “The biggest change is that it’s from all avenues of approach instead of just from the north, and it’s with systems that could affect us from further away. So therefore our defense capabilities need to be expanded further from our borders to make sure that we’re defending at the appropriate range.”
“What that necessitates is cooperation with EUCOM, PACOM, and SOUTHCOM, where we can exchange information, pictures, intelligence, and even resources to defend further away,” Guillot said.
VanHerck applauded efforts to strengthen Arctic security and stop threats before they reach North America.
“Homeland defense doesn’t start in the homeland,” VanHerck said. “It starts forward with allies and partners and fellow combat commanders forward. Ideally, you have a posture and a presence and enough domain awareness that you deter those activities before they ever start. And if they’re going to attack, you can defeat those adversaries or capabilities further forward.”
The Trump administration has made Arctic security a centerpiece of its foreign policy, pressing to win new concessions for American basing in Greenland, expanding beyond a single Space Force installation to establish two new bases. Demonstrating the critical nature of Greenland to North American security, the administration transferred responsibility for Greenland, a territory of Denmark, to U.S. Northern Command, removing it from U.S. European Command’s area of responsibility.
That transfer is far from symbolic. “A lot of exercises and operations that we would normally conduct either unilaterally, or perhaps with Canada through NORAD, we’re now doing with other countries to include Denmark,” Guillot said.
A recent exercise with the U.S. and allied nations marked the first time Danish F-35s landed in Greenland.
U.S., Canadian, and Danish forces conducted joint Operation Arctic Vanguard and NATO exercises in Greenland this month that drew F-35As from continental U.S. bases, U.S. F-16s from Alaska, Canadian CF-18s, and Danish F-35As. French air-to-air refueling aircraft and NATO-operated E-3 AWACS command-and-control jets also joined the operations as part of NATO’s Arctic Sentry.
Referencing the recent exercises, Guillot said allies were “fully integrated” and “operating in multiple lanes at the same time,” a shift from a few years ago when the U.S. may have conducted unilateral training instead. Operating as an integrated whole creates dilemmas for adversaries and acts as a force multiplier for the allies.
“That is possible due to the great relationship and partnering by the Danish forces,” Guillot said.
On the other side of North America, near Alaska, the U.S. and Canada recently conducted a joint exercise practicing striking maritime targets in the Bering Sea, using aircraft, surface vessels, and a submarine. The U.S. has also conducted joint naval operations with Canada that involve the U.S. Coast Guard alongside the U.S. military. Those exercises fall under Operation Tundra Merlin, which focuses on deterrence near Alaska, including the western Arctic and Northern Pacific. Pacific Air Forces aircraft stationed in Alaska also supported Arctic Vanguard on the other side of NORTHCOM’s region.
Alaska’s geographic size and placement at the nexus of the NORTHCOM and PACOM areas of responsibility places it in proximity to potential threats from China, Russia, and North Korea.
“I don’t think people appreciate the role that Alaska plays for our homeland defense mission, but also for our Indo-Pacific mission,” Ferguson said. “Alaska is critical as a place of power projection to be able to project power not only into the Indo-Pacific in the event of a contingency, but also into the European theater.”
The exercises underscore Guillot’s broader Nordic Bridge initiative, launched earlier this year to better integrate allied operations across the Arctic. It includes coordination among the various U.S. combatant commands that touch on the region, as well as Canada, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, Norway, and Iceland, all NATO allies. Working together, they aim to enhance domain awareness and interoperability.
“We’re working with other friendly Arctic nations to increase our presence,” Guillot said, “to increase and expand the deterrence, and make sure that every exercise we do up there is multinational and along multiple avenues of approach.”

articles.title: Poland boosts air defence after ‘Russian provocations’ amid Ukraine war
articles.body:
Poland boosts air defence after ‘Russian provocations’ amid Ukraine war
Alleged incursions put NATO nations on alert as Ukraine launches strikes on Russia during parliamentary voting.
Poland has heightened its air defence posture, following repeated alleged incursions into its airspace in recent weeks.
The Polish Air Force launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Zelenskyy says Ukraine sent two North Korean POWs to South Korea
- list 2 of 4Russian attacks kill eight people across Ukraine as US steps up diplomacy
- list 3 of 4Russia attacks Ukraine while Zelenskyy speaks at UNGA
- list 4 of 4US seeks to revive Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks as seven killed in Kyiv
Warsaw officially blamed Russia, but Moscow has denied allegations that it is targeting NATO nations.
“Following the latest Russian provocations and acts of aggression, I have made the decision to expand the protection of our airspace. We are increasing the activity of our air forces, including F-16 aircraft and helicopters,” wrote Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz on social media.
Those patrols came with a political warning.
“I want to present to the public the most probable scenario for the next few months, because it is a scenario that assumes serious events and requires focus, seriousness and the mental readiness to pass difficult exams,” said Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
“According to intelligence, the Russian plan also includes hybrid drone and missile strikes against countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland,” he said in parliament. “These possibilities have been mentioned for a long time, and today the information is very consistent and, unfortunately, convincing.”
He said the aim of suspected Russian incursions was “to weaken the motivation of NATO countries to apply NATO regulations in the event of aggression against any member state”.
Days later, on September 23, Poland said an Mi-8 helicopter entered Polish airspace from Kaliningrad for 42 seconds.
“Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence,” said Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command.
The most serious Polish claim of a violation was by a Russian Su-24 reconnaissance aircraft in the Baltic Sea in February 2025, an incident Russia reportedly acknowledged.
During the past week, suspected Russian drones were shot down twice in Moldova, and once in Romania on September 24, observers said.
Poland and Romania are two NATO members immediately bordering Ukraine through which military supplies and Western officials have reached Ukraine. Hungary is also a NATO member bordering Ukraine, but has not allowed military supplies through its territory.
The latest alleged airspace violations have again raised the spectre of an open Russian attack on NATO territory, a prospect European intelligence chiefs have been warning about since January 2024.
Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka this week told The Guardian that a Russian attack, which “could involve a limited incursion, false-flag provocations, [or] a massive influence campaign”, might come in a matter of “months, not years”.
Russian information, and reality
During the past week, Russian officials made claims to have captured towns in the eastern Ukrainian Donetsk region.
Russia’s Ministry of Defence said on September 19 Moscow’s forces had seized 5,300 square kilometres (2,050 square miles) and more than 220 settlements in Ukraine since the start of 2026.
Moscow launched drone strikes against Ukrainian cities every night of the week, and combined them with missiles on September 19, 22 and 24, killing at least eight people and injuring dozens. One of those deaths was a cleric at a monastery in Kherson. Two were killed when Russia launched three waves of ballistic missiles at Kyiv, including a maternity clinic.
“Since the beginning of this year, Russia has used more than 2,100 missiles of various types against Ukraine. More than 950 of these were ballistic missiles,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly. During the same period, Russia launched 63,000 drones into the country, he said.
“We need to slow it down before we move to the next stage,” he said. “Because next year, there is a real possibility that AI – not just humans – will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield.”
According to the Institute for the Study of War, which assesses territorial changes using geolocated open sources, Russian claims of a serious advance are vastly overstated.
It estimates that Russia has captured a net 147.7sq km (57sq miles) in the first eight months of 2026, its worst performance of the war by far. Ukrainian forces had liberated at least 972.56sq km (375sq miles) from Russian occupation during the same period, it has found.
Those counteroffensives have come near Oleksandrivka, straddling the Donetsk-Zaporizhia border, and around the town of Lyman in northern Donetsk.
The Lyman operation, codenamed Vivaldi, saw 50sq km (20sq miles) liberated in a second phase of the operation in recent days, Ukrainian officials said.
“Artillery and drone systems targeted enemy command posts, communication hubs, logistics, crossings, and reserves. Air defence and electronic warfare systems created a protective shield over the area of combat operations. The blinded enemy was unable to decipher the plan of the operation, and our units consolidated on the liberated lines,” said an announcement from the Third Army Corps commanded by Andriy Biletsky.
Russia’s vote, a referendum on the war
Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia Party triumphed in the Duma elections, raising its majority from 315 seats in the 450-seat body to 355.
Russian officials prejudged the result as a positive referendum on Putin’s war in Ukraine.
“I have no doubt that the result will confirm the commitment of all our parties and voters to the course the president has set both domestically and for our foreign policy,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters ahead of the election.
“We will continue to ensure support for our president’s course and bring victory over the enemies of the Fatherland closer,” deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev wrote on Russian social media.
Ukraine launched its biggest combined air strike of the war on the final day of Russia’s parliamentary elections.
Moscow mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on September 20 that Russian air defences downed more than 1,600 Ukrainian drones in the previous 24 hours, at least 450 of them heading for Moscow.
Some got through, putting Moscow’s oil refinery out of action for the second time this year. Videos posted online showed several fires, suggesting a number of successful strikes.
During the past week, Ukraine also struck the Kuybyshev refinery in Samara and the Bashneft refinery in Bashkortostan.

articles.title: Russian nuclear strike threat against Lithuania sparks alarm, then disappears
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday addressed for the first time European concerns that Russia could escalate its confrontation with Western European countries, categorically rejecting the possibility. At the same time, Putin offered a pessimistic assessment of prospects for progress toward a ceasefire in Ukraine, blaming a massive Ukrainian attack on Moscow during Russia's parliamentary "elections."
Responding to warnings voiced in Europe over the past week about the possibility of a direct military confrontation with Russia, Putin said: "Many in Europe say they expect an attack by the Russian Federation and therefore must prepare for military action, for war with Russia. I want to emphasize once again that we are not preparing for any military action against Europe. We have no such plans. Most importantly, there is no reason for it."
Putin nevertheless heightened tensions with the Baltic states by mocking a statement by Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem, who said his country must be prepared to repel any attack and "destroy anyone who crosses the border."
"This is a provocation," Putin said. "The circus has already left, but the clowns remain."
Putin's remarks came hours after Russia's state-run RIA Novosti news agency removed an opinion column in which the author threatened another Baltic state, Lithuania, with a blitzkrieg and nuclear strike. The column was removed after several hours, with the agency saying it did not conform to its editorial position or the official policy of the Russian Federation.
One scenario raised in the West this week is that Russia and its ally Belarus could attempt to seize the Suwalki Gap, the strip of territory between Poland and Lithuania that separates Belarus from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and provides the Baltic states' only land connection to the rest of NATO.
The deleted column was written by commentator Alexander Nosovich after Lithuania's parliament moved this week to advance a proposal that would lift the country's ban on stationing nuclear weapons on its territory.
The column, headlined "Russia is in for another special military operation. It will be very short," said in part: "European countries continue to push the issue of moving unconventional weapons to Russia's borders and have chosen a country willing to become a nuclear depot."
Nosovich went on to threaten Lithuania with an invasion and even a nuclear strike.
"Russia can even afford to forgo deploying ground troops. Just missiles with the appropriate warheads," he wrote. "The solution is not merely quick, it is lightning-fast. Don't think too much about seconds."
Elsewhere in the column, Nosovich described Lithuania as "a suicidal country with no brains whatsoever," a "useful idiot" and "a small but proud kamikaze in Russia's near abroad."
Shortly after publication, however, the column was deleted. Anyone visiting the original link on RIA Novosti's website encountered an editor's note saying: "The article by freelance author Alexander Nosovich was removed from the website because it did not correspond to the editorial board's views, editorial policy or the official policy of the Russian Federation."
Before it was removed, the threatening column circulated on social media and caused alarm among parts of the Lithuanian public. An official Lithuanian military spokesperson issued a statement seeking to reassure the public: "In light of Russia's propaganda statement, we remind you that Russia routinely tries to intimidate its neighbors using hostile rhetoric. This is a common Russian practice, and no additional action should be taken as a result of these remarks."
Over the past roughly 35 years, Russia has lost much of its strategic position around the Baltic Sea. The former Soviet republics of Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia joined NATO in the early 2000s. About two decades later, Finland and Sweden abandoned decades of military nonalignment and joined the alliance. Russia's Baltic Sea coastline now includes the Kaliningrad exclave, whose land connections to the rest of Russia require transit through neighboring countries.
'Ukraine as cannon fodder'
Turning to the war in Ukraine, Putin said Friday that before there could be progress toward a settlement, Kyiv must "feel the power of Russia's retaliatory strikes" following Ukraine's massive drone attack on Moscow this week.
The Ukrainian attack came on the final day of Russia's parliamentary "elections," in which Putin's United Russia party won as expected.
"Polling stations were attacked," Putin said. "One of the attacks targeted a school where there was a polling station. They began attacking the homes of regional election commission chairs. In one case, a regional commission chair was wounded, her husband was wounded and her child was wounded. In another case, unfortunately, it ended in tragedy and an election commission chair was killed. We must make Kyiv understand that strikes deep inside Russian territory will only make the situation worse."
Addressing the role of Western European countries in the war in Ukraine, Putin said: "They want Ukraine to continue serving as cannon fodder, as a tool in the struggle against Russia."
Putin also showed no willingness to accept a proposal to halt reciprocal attacks on energy facilities in Russia and Ukraine.
"They have no means to counter our advanced weapons or to end the blockade we have imposed on their Black Sea coast," he said. "They need to remember that they are the ones who started all of this."

articles.title: Iran awaits US response on plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran awaited a formal U.S. response Saturday to a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and halt fighting across the Middle East, after The Wall Street Journal reported that President Donald Trump had rejected the initiative.
The proposal, presented by Iran at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and conveyed to Washington through Qatari mediators, calls for a pause in hostilities and the eventual reopening of the strategic waterway, a vital route for global energy shipments.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Friday that Tehran had prepared the framework for a deal and was ready to move quickly if Washington showed a willingness to reach an agreement.
"If there is seriousness on the U.S. side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," Araqchi told reporters at the United Nations.
But the Journal, citing unnamed U.S. officials, reported that Trump was privately skeptical that Tehran would meet his demands and had told aides that he expected a renewed bombing campaign after the November midterm elections.
Reuters could not immediately independently confirm the Journal's report. Earlier, a U.S. official said discussions with Iran through mediators had been "positive and constructive."
Under Tehran's proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz after a seven-day period during which hostilities would be halted across the region, including in Lebanon.
In return, Araqchi said Washington would have to lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian funds and waive oil sanctions.
If those conditions were accepted, the two sides could move into broader negotiations on issues they mutually agree to discuss, potentially including Iran's nuclear program.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran would not make concessions on what it considers its nuclear rights, including uranium enrichment or the transfer of its highly enriched uranium out of the country. The official said the strait would remain closed until Washington met all of Iran's conditions.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in an interview with CBS' "Face the Nation" that Tehran was prepared to negotiate on its nuclear program and other issues but would not accept what he described as "bullying or coercion."
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks," Pezeshkian said.
He also said Iran had already agreed that it should not develop nuclear weapons.
Trump has repeatedly said Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon. Tehran has denied seeking one.
The diplomatic effort comes after months of fighting that have disrupted energy shipments and intensified pressure on economies across the region.
The conflict began Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran and has since moved through periods of reduced fighting followed by renewed strikes. The fighting has killed thousands, weakened Iran's conventional military capabilities and placed additional strain on its economy.
Iran and allied groups have also expanded attacks across the region.
The Strait of Hormuz has become a central pressure point in the conflict because of its importance to global energy markets. Before the war, the waterway carried roughly a fifth of global oil and gas shipments, making its disruption a major concern for energy markets and international trade.
Iran shares control of the strategic waterway with Oman and has used its position there as leverage in negotiations with Washington.
Tehran has also opened communication with its longtime regional rival Saudi Arabia over shipping through the strait.
Araqchi briefed Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan on an understanding between Iran and Oman concerning safe shipping routes, according to Iran's Foreign Ministry.
The outreach comes as Saudi Arabia faces a growing security threat from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
The Houthis have launched missiles and drones toward Saudi territory and have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea. The attacks have added another layer of risk to regional energy supplies while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains heavily disrupted.
Saudi-led forces said Saturday that they had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched toward Khamis Mushait and two drones headed toward Riyadh.
The Houthi attacks have also raised concerns over the Red Sea, an alternative route for Gulf energy exports when traffic through Hormuz is restricted.
The widening conflict has pushed Saudi Arabia and its partners to strengthen military coordination.
Defense officials from Türkiye and Pakistan met in Riyadh on Friday with Saudi counterparts to discuss intelligence cooperation, military coordination and the integration of forces, according to Saudi Arabia's Defense Ministry.
The meeting followed talks between the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers under the framework of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
The escalation has also deepened humanitarian concerns in Yemen.
UNICEF said Friday that acute malnutrition among children was rising as renewed violence worsened conditions in the country.

articles.title: Russia’s air defenses can’t protect all its strategic sites once Ukraine’s ballistic missiles are ready, expert says
articles.body:
Russia's best defenses against ballistic missiles ring Moscow, leaving much of the rest of the country exposed to Ukraine's growing missile arsenal. That concentration is why Ukraine's homegrown ballistic missiles could cause Russia real trouble beyond the capital, even as Russia's air defenses show gaps elsewhere, expert Vadym Kushnikov says, Ukrainian Radio reports.
Russia has the systems to stop ballistic missiles, Kushnikov continues, but it has massed the best of them around Moscow: the S-500 "Prometey", with interceptors adapted from the A-135, the Soviet-era shield built to defend the capital from missiles.
Other regions, by his assessment, are left more open to Ukraine's massed and combined strikes. That matters now that Ukraine's own ballistic missile, such as the Sapsan, is entering combat.
The best defenses ring Moscow
"If you analyze the characteristics, Russia today has concentrated its most modern S-500 complexes, with 77N6-N and 77N6-N1 interceptors, in Moscow Oblast," Kushnikov says.
Elsewhere, he said, Russia is short of air-defense complexes, the S-400 among them, a shortfall he said is visible in satellite imagery.
Ukraine's ballistic program grows
Ukraine's deep-strike arsenal has been shifting from foreign-supplied systems to homegrown ones. Alongside its Neptune and Flamingo cruise missiles, it now fields the Sapsan, an Iskander-class ballistic missile with a range of about 500 kilometers, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed was in combat late last year.
A domestic ballistic missile will let Ukraine strike deep inside Russia without waiting for a Western green light.
Production faces hard hurdles
Building them is the hard part. Ukraine's rocket-engineering tradition runs deep, Kushnikov suggests, but its production sites, mostly in the east, are direct targets of Russian strikes.
The missiles also depend on components that are difficult to make, chiefly solid-fuel rocket engines and the guidance that steers a warhead flying at five times the speed of sound along a ballistic arc.
"The combination of all these factors is exactly what our engineers have worked on for years, building the Ukrainian ballistic shield," he adds.

articles.title: Iran awaits US reply to seven-day Hormuz plan
articles.body:
Iran awaited an official U.S. response on Sept. 26 to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, after The Wall Street Journal reported that President Donald Trump had rejected the offer.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the proposal, delivered through Qatar, required Washington to meet conditions set out in a memorandum of understanding signed in June.
“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” he told reporters at the United Nations in New York on Sept. 25.
“The choice now rests with the United States,” he added.
Araghchi did not detail the steps Iran wanted Washington to take, saying they were already covered by the June agreement.
The Journal, citing U.S. officials, reported that Trump had told aides he expected to resume bombing Iran after November’s midterm elections.
Earlier, a U.S. official told the BBC that discussions through mediators were positive and included nuclear issues, while saying Washington was “not in a rush.”
In a CBS News interview, President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran would allow nuclear inspectors to return, with arrangements to be negotiated.
The June 18 memorandum called for an end to military operations on all fronts, sanctions relief and the lifting of the U.S. naval blockade. It also included provisions for restoring commercial shipping through Hormuz and Iran’s commitment not to acquire nuclear weapons.
The agreement broke down after both sides resumed strikes.
The United States and Israel began strikes on Iran on Feb. 28. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel, U.S. bases and Gulf countries, while blocking Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas before the war.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said on Sept. 26 that it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Iran-backed Houthis toward Khamis Mushait and two drones heading toward Riyadh.

articles.title: Iran, Russia, China must set up a balanced structure in BRICS
articles.body:
To learn more about the details, Mehr news agency's correspondent has conducted an interview with Dr. Leonid Savin Editor-in-Chief and Managing Director of Katehon, an influential Russian Think Tank.
Let’s review the interview in questions and answers.
Q: Given Russia’s conduct since the outbreak of the US-Israeli war against Iran, how would you assess Moscow’s approach and actions in the political, diplomatic, military, and intelligence spheres? To what extent have these actions been consistent with Tehran’s expectations of a strategic partner?
A: First of all, Russia and Iran signed new special agreement some time ago that bring our partnership into new level of cooperation. On diplomatic international level Russia supports Iran for different spheres of activity – from rejection of foreign interference and imposed sanctions to justification of nuclear program of Iran (and Russia is involved into construction process of Busher plant). Military and intelligence coordination is not open for public. We know about some supplies of Russian technics and equipment like aircrafts and helicopters. And before Iran provided to Russia drone technologies (“Sheheed” model that in Russia got name “Geran” and then developed for reactive strike drone). Western media also blame Russia for providing to Iran data intelligence, cause of space surveillance available for Russian military. But real scale of military/intelligence cooperation is unknown cause of sensitive information and secret issues. Counter-terrorism interaction also was always on high level and this activity
Personally, I think that both countries can and need to do more to enlarge bilateral partnership. To organize defense pact, at least for Caspian region
Q: Some argue that Russia has acted cautiously in response to the war against Iran. Is this caution primarily driven by Russia’s involvement in the war in Ukraine and its concerns about a direct confrontation with the United States, or does Moscow fundamentally seek to avoid becoming involved in a war that could put its own interests at risk?
A: We understand very well, that the collective West interested to destroy Russia by any means. The same strategy used against Iran. China also seems for the West like potential adversary and before there were many attempts to bring domestic problems for the China through different tools of manipulations. Also, Ukrainian conflict by fact is proxy war against Russia led by the West. The most significant role in support of Kiev’s regime and against Russia played by leaders of the UK, USA, France and Germany. BBC team organized fake report about Bucha in 2022 when Russian troops was withdrawal. In general, political elites of the West always tried to deceive Russian leadership and there no any trust anymore.
Also, we understand risk of escalation till nuclear war. And would like to avoid it. But if the West and his proxies will do more provocations against Russia (and they do it in regular way) Moscow will need to do response. From this point of view Russian interests mostly focused on keeping unity and secure periphery as well as technological development and achievement of the full independence (autarky). Of course, another important strategic line is army reorganization to be more effective and use of advanced weapon systems. Defense ministry and corporations linked with military industrial production now care about it. Ukrainian conflict was and still experience for Russian military and security services.
Q: With Trump’s return to office, there was widespread speculation in the media that Russia and Ukraine were moving closer to a ceasefire agreement, but such an agreement ultimately failed to materialize. In your view, what were the main obstacles to a ceasefire between the two sides? Was the dispute over territory and security guarantees the primary issue, or does the disagreement run deeper, involving fundamentally different views about the future of European security and Russia’s relationship with the West?
A: It never was closer. Russia ready to sign peace agreement but only on conditions proposed before – denazification and demilitarization of Ukraine, respect of Russian geopolitical interests and organization of clear security frame. Ukraine cannot be member of NATO. Russian people in Ukraine must be respected and their right respected. As well as about Russian Orthodox Church in Ukraine. Crimea and regions of ex-Ukraine where people voted to be with Russia as its part will stay in Russia and will never return to Ukraine. Actually, from European point of view, it is not violation cause after 1999 when part of Serbia (Kosovo) proclaimed self-independence, it was supported by NATO and the West. So, what we see in Ukraine now is just continuation of the policy once used by the West.
Concerning Russian view on future we are more interested to develop active relationship with Global South. There was term like “Turn to the East”, but really to the South too. And Iran is also part of it.
Q: In light of the war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war against Iran, and increasing US pressure on China, does Moscow view these developments as separate crises, or does it see them as part of a broader strategic competition between the United States and non-Western powers, as well as an effort to reshape the existing international order?
A: Of course, it is strategic competition effected by emergence of the multipolar world order. West led by the US just would like to keep own hegemony (military, political, economic and also moral). We are wanting more justice international system. This is the reason. If you see on historical perspectives there were the same disturbance during transition from one type of order to another. But now multipolar moment is unique cause the West losing his dominance like never before.
Q: How would you assess Iran’s response and resistance to the US and Israeli attacks? In your view, to what extent has Iran been able to maintain the initiative, withstand military pressure, and influence the calculations of its adversaries during this confrontation?
A: It is very appreciated and Russian public applause to Iran, especially to decision makers for this response. It was very strong and at the same time very smart. To block Hormuz strait was geopolitical nightmare for the US and its allies in region. Both the US and Israel understood own misfortune over Iran. Despite own victims resulted by illegal and criminal strikes of the US and Israel Iran and its people stands firm.
Q: Could the war against Iran become a turning point in the security order of the Middle East? If so, what role does Russia envision for itself in the emerging regional order, and how might Moscow’s relations with Iran, China, and the United States change in the aftermath of the war?
A: For my opinion it is already changed security environment of the region. And neighbor countries already reacted on this change, I mean Mecca pact between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. Iran also projected new lines of control and interests near own borders. We can add allies of Iran in Yemen, but also in Iraq, Lebanon and other countries. Zionists would like to eliminate them all and it is the reason of genocide in Palestine and bombing Lebanon, but in practice it is not possible. Like decades before resistance will be revived because of the mentality and strategic culture.
If speak about relations of great powers there is clear that Russia and China will continue to strengthen cooperation. But the US will have more problems in future. Geopolitical influence of the US in the Middle East will decline. Many partners inside NATO not trust to the Washington anymore. There also tensions because Israeli lobby and part of politicians inside the US not welcome this trend. Let’s see what happens after November elections in the Congress. There are many signs that against Trump growing antipathy in camp of Republicans and Democrats also not happy with his policy.
Realistically there still will be tensions and conflict. To achieve multipolarity we need to create effective structure. Why it is important? Because unipolar world still has it – World bank and IMF in economy, NATO in military, G7 politically. So, Russia, China, Iran, other members of BRICS need to create counter balance, effective and complete.
MNA

articles.title: The global system is entering an age of technological entropy
articles.body:
The global system is entering an age of technological entropy
The “profound changes unseen in a century” often mentioned by Xi Jinping are no longer merely abstract concepts found in books; they represent the systemic collapse and restructuring currently experienced by the global system.
For centuries, the world operated under a singular order – dominated by the West, characterized by linear development and a hegemonic steady state – which established fixed power structures, rules of engagement, and development paradigms. As we enter the second quarter of the 21st century, this long-standing old order has reached a critical juncture marked by runaway entropy, the collapse of paradigms, and a civilizational transition.
This entropic shift of order is essentially a global transitional state where the rules of the old system fail, its structures loosen, and its momentum wanes, while a new system undergoes pluralistic growth and iterative restructuring without yet having fully crystallized. Unlike the traditional restructuring of global patterns seen in historical dynastic changes or great-power rivalries, the core transformation of this ‘once-in-a-century’ shift is driven by the convergence of three forces: the fundamental reshaping of technology, the shifting of geopolitical centers of gravity, and the escalation of strategic competition to higher dimensions. Together, these forces are driving a comprehensive, systemic iteration of global politics, military affairs, economics, public opinion, and governance.
Adopting a holistic perspective, this article systematically deconstructs the core characteristics, underlying operational logic, and certain future evolutionary trends of this global entropic shift. Moving beyond the interpretation of fragmented events, it identifies the fundamental laws and ultimate trajectory of the transformation of the global landscape in this new era.
I. Six core characteristics of the entropic shift of order: The disintegration of the old steady state and the normalization of global pluralistic disorder
Current global geopolitical conflicts, economic fluctuations, technological rivalries, and public opinion polarization are, in essence, concrete manifestations of this entropic shift in order. The steady-state equilibrium established by the traditional Western-centric order has completely disintegrated. The global landscape now exhibits four core characteristics: intensifying headwinds, accelerating fragmentation, the resonance of risks, and the generalization of strategic competition. Uncertainty, asymmetry, and cross-domain transmission have become the new normal of the global landscape.
First, geopolitical power has undergone complete decentralization, and the absolute advantages once held by traditional major powers have fully eroded.
The geopolitical logic that prevailed for a century – where victory was determined by sheer national scale, military force, or resource endowment – has become completely obsolete; technological democratization has emerged as the core variable reshaping regional landscapes.
In the core geopolitical regions of Eurasia and the Middle East, the large-scale deployment of artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons, and intelligent reconnaissance systems has drastically lowered the threshold for war and deterrence, effectively erasing the military ‘generation gap’ that once separated traditional major powers. Europe’s security landscape has moved beyond the US monopoly; France and Germany are pursuing strategic autonomy, while Russia is leveraging intelligent hardware to challenge Western military hegemony, leading to a stratification and fragmentation of regional power. The Middle East has completely shed the old order defined by resource dominance and control by major powers; small and medium-sized states – and even non-state actors like the Houthis – can now exert asymmetric influence and disrupt regional shipping and geopolitics using low-cost intelligent equipment, causing the absolute control once held by major powers to steadily crumble.
Geopolitical power is no longer tethered to territory, troop numbers, or resource volume; instead, it is anchored in technological computing power, intelligent warfare capabilities, and the pace of technological iteration. Global geopolitical rivalry has entered a new phase where small nations can act as counterweights and non-state actors can disrupt the status quo.
Second, strategic deterrence systems have become stratified and diffuse, shifting global security risks from great-power confrontation to a state of uncontrolled volatility across all domains.
The ‘balance of terror’ established by the rigid US-Soviet bipolar nuclear standoff during the Cold War has collapsed, marking a paradigm shift in the global nuclear landscape; nuclear weapons have evolved from an ultimate deterrent for total mutual restraint into leverage for controlling regional dynamics.
Nuclear deterrence is now clearly stratified: Top-tier nuclear powers maintain a strategic last-resort capability while avoiding direct hot wars; mid-tier nuclear states rely on limited arsenals for regional self-preservation; and non-nuclear states seek security under the umbrella of major powers. Nuclear rivalry has become instrumentalized and normalized, serving as a standard tool for major powers to draw red lines and signal strategic intent.
Meanwhile, nuclear risks have become widespread; while the likelihood of direct nuclear confrontation between major powers has declined, risks associated with proliferation, technology leaks, algorithmic miscalculation, and covert regional nuclear maneuvering are rising. Compounded by the deep integration of intelligent weaponry and nuclear technology, global security governance has shifted from a model of great-power checks and balances to a complex challenge of managing risks that are multidimensional, covert, and pervasive across all domains.
Third, the global development landscape is shifting from West to East, and the Western-centric system that has prevailed for five centuries is unraveling.
The most historic transformation in this round of upheaval is the holistic shift of the global geopolitical, economic, and civilizational center of gravity from the Atlantic to the Eurasian landmass and Asia as a whole, fundamentally overturning the underlying structure of Western global dominance that has persisted for five centuries.
Economically, the interconnected development of Asian blocs – including China, ASEAN, India, and the Middle East – is accelerating the formation of a pan-Eurasian economic cycle; the era of Western dominance over global supply chains, trade rules, and economic orders is drawing to a close, while the Global South is gaining a powerful voice in development discourse. Regarding security, the security landscapes of Europe, the Middle East, and the Asia-Pacific are becoming deeply intertwined; the geopolitical value of the continental landmass is making a full comeback, while the reach and control of traditional maritime hegemony continue to wane.
In terms of civilization and governance, Asian concepts of diverse coexistence and mutually beneficial cooperation are countering the Western logic of zero-sum hegemony; the resurgence of diverse civilizations is breaking the Western monopoly on civilization, emerging multilateral mechanisms are gradually replacing traditional Western-led institutions, and the pluralistic nature of global governance is becoming increasingly distinct.
Fourth, the credibility of the hegemonic system has collapsed, and the Western-led global rules-based system has comprehensively failed.
Trump’s transactional ‘America First’ diplomacy served as the critical turning point that broke the back of American-style hegemony, definitively ending the era of absolute US unilateral global control. The foundations of US hegemony – built after World War II upon alliance systems, rule-setting dominance, and the provision of public goods – have been thoroughly dismantled; alliance credibility has been squandered, multilateral systems have eroded, and the globalized order has fractured, transforming the US from an order builder into an order destroyer.
Although the Biden administration briefly attempted remedial measures, these failed to restore US credibility. Global deficits in trust and institutional confidence regarding the US have become entrenched; unilateralism and protectionism run rampant, double standards in traditional international rules have become glaring, and global governance has fallen into a vacuum of entropic change – where old rules have failed but new ones have yet to be established.
Fifth, the dimension of state-level rivalry has undergone a comprehensive escalation, with the battle for perception and public opinion emerging as a core, invisible battlefield.
The proliferation of digital technology has fundamentally restructured the model of great-power competition, shifting the focus of rivalry from traditional physical confrontation to precision-targeted cognitive warfare. Technologies such as 5G, algorithmic recommendation, and big-data profiling have constructed an information ecosystem characterized by pervasive reach, the solidification of echo chambers, and emotional dominance.
Leveraging their long-standing monopoly on discourse, the US and the West continuously export polarizing narratives, manufacture bloc-based confrontations, and fracture social consensus in other nations. The digital era has dismantled the official barriers of traditional diplomacy; ordinary citizens and non-governmental entities have become pivotal nodes in the global strategic game, with public sentiment and perception directly influencing geopolitical dynamics and diplomatic decisions. Public opinion manipulation and the shaping of perceptions achieve the strategic goal of subduing the enemy without fighting, while cognitive polarization and public opinion divides have become major drivers of disorder in the global order.
Sixth, the key actors in the global economy and governance are undergoing a comprehensive transformation, completely shattering traditional monopolistic patterns.
In the economic sphere, the traditional globalization model – which prioritized efficiency above all – has become obsolete. Geopolitical conflicts, technological blockades, and investment barriers are forcing the global economy to shift toward a development logic that prioritizes resilience and regional self-containment; regional integration is replacing global integration as a core mechanism for hedging against risk, while emerging markets and the Global South have become key stabilizers of the global economy.
In the realm of governance, the effectiveness of traditional Western-dominated institutions – such as the UN, IMF, and World Bank – is steadily declining, whereas emerging multilateral platforms like the SCO, BRICS, and G20 are rising rapidly. Global conflict resolution models are shifting from Western-led coercive intervention to diverse, consultative, and cooperative governance. Simultaneously, the global influence of non-governmental forces and industry elites continues to grow, shifting the landscape of global governance actors from one dominated solely by sovereign states to a new pattern of coexistence among governments, international institutions, and non-governmental entities.
II. Four new operational logics of order reconstruction: A new-era strategic paradigm breaking free from Western conventions
The entropic shift in the global order signifies far more than mere turbulence; it represents a fundamental and disruptive transformation of the underlying logic governing global operations. Current global competition, cooperation, and conflict can no longer be explained by the outdated Western realist paradigms of hegemony through strength, zero-sum games, and victory through force.
A new operational logic – tailored to a multipolar, digital, and regionalized world – has taken shape, fundamentally rewriting the underlying rules governing the rise of major powers, regional development, and global governance.
First, the logic of core national power: A shift from dominance through sheer scale to victory through technology and resilience.
Traditional international competition was a contest of sheer scale – territorial size, military tonnage, and aggregate economic output – whereby major powers could leverage their massive size to establish hegemonic monopolies and exert unilateral dominance. In the current era of shifting order and entropy, however, the primary benchmarks for a nation’s core competitiveness have become technological computing power, the capacity for intelligent iteration, supply chain resilience, and the ability to withstand risks.
Intelligent weaponry is reshaping the military balance of power; digital technology governs the discourse on public opinion and perception; autonomous industrial chains hedge against the risks of geopolitical sanctions; and regional closed-loop economic systems buffer against global volatility. Small and medium-sized nations can achieve asymmetric checks and balances through breakthroughs in specific technologies. Conversely, without technological innovation and systemic resilience, a major power’s sheer size risks becoming an inefficient burden – a reality that fundamentally shatters the Western historical logic equating size with hegemony.
Secondly, the logic of great power rise: shifting from hegemonic succession to rule reshaping.
Centuries of Western historical narrative have entrenched a realist paradigm – that rising implies conflict, growing strength implies a bid for dominance, and hegemony inevitably changes hands. Indeed, all Western international relations theories are essentially distillations of the history of European colonial rivalry. Yet, the current restructuring of the global landscape has completely transcended the old trap of hegemonic cycles.
The rise of emerging powers – exemplified by China – eschews military expansion, the pursuit of hegemonic status, and bloc-based confrontation; instead, it achieves developmental breakthroughs through civilizational mutual learning, regional synergy, and mutually beneficial cooperation. At its peak, the Tang Dynasty accounted for 80% of Asia’s GDP, and Zheng He’s fleet was ten times the size of Columbus’; despite possessing such overwhelming strength, China never followed the Western path of colonial conquest or regional monopoly. This proves that strength does not equate to hegemony, nor does rising equate to conflict; an Eastern logic of symbiosis is replacing the Western logic of dominance-seeking, establishing a brand-new paradigm for the rise of great powers.
Thirdly, the logic of security and stability: shifting from external balancing to autonomous resilience.
Since the Cold War, global security has maintained a precarious equilibrium based on great-power standoffs, alliance entanglements, and the balancing of forces. Control over the security agenda rested in the hands of a few Western powers, leaving most nations with no choice but to attach themselves to the strong and passively seek to avoid risk. In this era of entropic shifts in the global order, security risks have become diffuse and unpredictable, and the stability provided by external checks and balances has completely collapsed; consequently, autonomy and controllability, diversified hedging strategies, and systemic resilience have become the core pillars of security.
Militarily, nations are building autonomous defense systems powered by intelligent technologies; economically, they are establishing regional closed-loop industrial chains to mitigate the risks of decoupling; financially, they are promoting local currency settlements to hedge against the weaponization of the US dollar; and in the realm of public opinion, they are constructing independent discourse systems to break cognitive monopolies. Nations are moving away from reliance on the protection of major powers, instead seizing the initiative in their own security and development by leveraging systemic resilience and regional cooperation.
Fourth, the logic of global governance is shifting from Western monopoly to pluralistic, shared governance.
Traditional global governance was a game dominated by a handful of Western developed nations – where rules were set, standards defined, and benefits monopolized by the West, leaving developing countries to merely accept and adapt passively. The entropic shift in the global order has shattered this monopoly; the collective rise of the Global South and the growing influence of emerging multilateral mechanisms have led to a comprehensive diversification of governance actors, rules, and philosophies.
The core of governance has shifted from the strong controlling the weak to equal consultation among diverse actors; rules have evolved from self-serving Western unilateral standards into win-win principles that prioritize fairness and broad-based benefits; and the logic of development has moved beyond zero-sum plunder toward inclusive coexistence and mutual learning, marking the true entry of global governance into a new era of multilateralism.
III. Future trajectory of global order entropy change: Multipolar consolidation, resilient symbiosis, and the restoration of civilizational roles
While the current entropy change in the global order appears chaotic and fraught with risk, it is by no means random turbulence or internal attrition; rather, it represents the inevitable growing pains accompanying the demise of the old order and the birth of the new. By grounding our analysis in the fundamental logic of this transformation, we can clearly foresee the major trends of global evolution over the coming decades. Three certain trends will dominate the global landscape during the second quarter of the 21st century, effectively ending the old era of Western-centric hegemony.
First, the global landscape will shift decisively from unipolar volatility to a multipolar steady state, with hegemonic influence undergoing a continuous and irreversible decline.
The era of absolute US hegemony has definitively ended. While American hegemony will not collapse overnight, it will continue to contract and decline in relative terms, shifting from a position of global dominance to that of a regional player. The global balance of power will continue to equalize; Asia’s status as a geopolitical center will be further consolidated, and the integration of the Eurasian landmass will steadily advance.
Deep interconnectedness among Asian blocs – including China, ASEAN, India, and the Middle East – will forge a cluster of emerging powers capable of acting as a counterweight to the Western system. Old models of bloc confrontation and zero-sum games will gradually fade, giving way to a mainstream global political landscape defined by great-power competition and cooperation, diversified checks and balances, and regional autonomy. Multipolarity will evolve from a mere trend into a solidified, stable global order.
Second, global development will shift decisively from efficiency-first to resilience-first, leading to the full formation of regional symbiotic systems.
Globalization will not disappear, but it will undergo a fundamental transformation and upgrade. The old model of globalization – characterized by extensive growth, homogenization, and Western dominance – is ending, while a new model defined by precision, regionalization, and diversification is rising. Nations will continue to diversify, localize, and autonomize their industrial and supply chains, prioritizing security and stability.
Regional economic synergy and closed-loop systems will serve as the core pillars for hedging against geopolitical conflicts, trade protectionism, and technological blockades. Emerging regional mechanisms – such as RCEP, SCO economic cooperation, and BRICS cooperation – will continue to enhance quality and efficiency, building regional development systems that are mutually beneficial and independent of the West. The global economy will break free from the constraints of singular Western rules, establishing a new development landscape characterized by diverse, parallel paths and resilient symbiosis.
Third, global competition is shifting profoundly from physical confrontation to a contest of rules and civilizations, marking a comprehensive resurgence of Eastern civilizational values.
The core of future great-power competition will no longer lie in military might, territorial disputes, or resource plundering, but in the ultimate contest over technological standards, governance norms, civilizational paradigms, and cognitive narratives. The flaws of the Western civilizational logic – characterized by zero-sum games, hegemony, and confrontation – have become glaringly apparent, rendering it ill-suited to the development needs of a diverse world.
In contrast, the Asia-Pacific region’s enduring civilizational ethos – rooted in mutual learning, symbiosis, harmony amid diversity, and win-win cooperation – will serve as the core foundation for reshaping the global civilizational order. From the millennia-old legacies of Xuanzang’s translation work, Yang Liangyao’s diplomatic voyages, and Zheng He’s friendly expeditions, to the vibrant contemporary practices of mutual learning and people-to-people connectivity across the Asia-Pacific, this Eastern civilization of symbiosis will continue to counter Western narratives of conflict and rewrite the fundamental rules of global civilizational competition.
Fourth, global governance is transitioning from elite monopoly to broad-based participation, with fairness and inclusivity becoming the prevailing trends of the era.
Future global governance will thoroughly dismantle the monopoly held by a handful of Western nations and elites; the Global South will see a sustained rise in its voice and influence, emerging multilateral mechanisms will become the primary vehicles for governance, and the participation of non-governmental actors and civil society will deepen.
Global public issues – such as nuclear arms control, artificial intelligence, climate governance, and public health – will break free from the constraints of geopolitical maneuvering and bloc-based confrontation, returning to the essence of multilateral consultation and win-win cooperation. Global governance will cease to be a tool for the powerful and instead become a platform for the shared development of all humanity, with fairness, inclusivity, and mutual benefit defining the new era of global governance.
Embracing the right path of Eastern symbiosis amid order reconstruction
Viewed from a macro perspective, the essence of this once-in-a-century transformation is a process – spanning centuries – of correcting the order, restoring the civilizational balance, and reshaping the global landscape. The entropic shift in the global order represents both the entropic decay and demise of the old Western hegemonic order and the entropic reduction and rebirth of a new, diverse global order.
All geopolitical conflicts, technological rivalries, economic fluctuations, and public opinion rifts are the inevitable growing pains accompanying the transition from the old order to the new. Centuries of Western history have taught the world only about hegemonic rivalry among the strong, whereas the Asia-Pacific region – with its millennia-old cultural heritage and the practical experience of emerging powers in the new era – is teaching the world how the strong can build bridges.
Future global competition is by no means a zero-sum game of hegemonic succession; rather, it is a contest of values regarding paths, civilizations, and rules. The old era defined by unilateralism, bloc confrontation, and zero-sum games has come to an end, while a new era characterized by multilateralism, openness, inclusiveness, and mutually beneficial symbiosis is rapidly unfolding.
Standing at the historical juncture of the second quarter of the 21st century, humanity will ultimately break free from the confines of the Western-dominated order and the traps of realist power struggles. By solidifying the foundations of development through technological innovation, fostering symbiotic strength through regional synergy, and resolving differences through mutual learning among civilizations, we will build a new global order that is fairer, more stable, more resilient, and more prosperous – thereby ushering in a new stage of civilization defined by diverse coexistence and sustainable development.

articles.title: Saudi hosts emergency Yemen talks; Iran submits new peace plan
articles.body:
We're closing this live page now.
Join us back here from 0900 tomorrow for more live coverage of developments in the Middle East.
Thanks for following.
Hello and welcome to our new live page where we're continuing to monitor developments in the Middle East.
You can catch up on developments earlier today by visiting our previous live page here.
Here are the key updates on Friday afternoon:
• Saudi, Turkey and Pakistan military chief held an urgent meeting to discuss the ongoing Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
• Members of the UN Security Council condemned "in the strongest terms" the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia.
• Iran has submitted a proposal to the US to end the US-Israeli war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days.
• Iraq's Najaf airport, a top destination for Shia pilgrims, suspended all Iranian flights on Friday under pressure from US sanctions.
• Colombia's new far-right, US-backed government has cut diplomatic ties with Iran.
The United States is having positive, constructive discussions with Iran through mediators and continues to discuss nuclear issues, a US official said on Friday when asked about Iran's proposed seven-day plan.
Iran has given the United States a "concrete" seven-day plan to open the strategic Strait of Hormuz and the choice now rests with the US, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations on Friday.
"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States," he said.
"The actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU," he said, referring to the memorandum of understanding that Iran and the United States agreed in June.
The military chiefs of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey discussed enhancing intelligence sharing, military coordination and capability integration at a meeting in Riyadh, the Pakistan military said on Saturday.
The chiefs reviewed the security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia, affirmed a commitment to collective defense and vowed to turn Mecca Joint Defense Agreement commitments into effective cooperation, the Pakistan military added.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Friday that his country wanted to return to the memorandum of understanding agreed with the United States in June, days after saying his country would not bend to Washington.
He welcomed China saying it wanted the agreement to be revived, posting on X that "Iran shares this approach and underscores the importance of returning to that understanding".
Diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the Middle East war, launched by the US and Israel with surprise attacks on Iran in late February, have faltered for months.
The June deal aimed to lay the ground for a full peace deal but it quickly unravelled.
There had been optimism that talks might be revived during the UN General Assembly this week, but in a defiant speech to the world body on Wednesday, Pezeshkian said Iran would not "bend at the knee" to the US.
A day later he told Fox News that Iran did "not wish to continue" the war but it was up to Washington to end it.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi took part in a meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff and presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner on the sidelines of the General Assembly, but their talks did not immediately yield a breakthrough.
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shebaz Sharif condemned Israel's "genocidal agenda" against the Palestinians and its aggression against Lebanon and Syria during his address at the UN General Assembly on Friday.
He also expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, which has faced what he called "deplorable attacks" by the Houthis in Yemen.
Torrential rains caused severe flooding across several towns in western Libya overnight Friday, cutting electricity and running water and trapping residents in torrents of mud.
Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah ordered authorities to immediately mobilise resources in affected areas "to ensure a rapid response", his office said.
Videos and images circulated on social media showed people trapped in vehicles or trying to escape the mudflows.
In Mizda, a town of fewer than 30,000 people in a semi-desert area south of Tripoli where heavy rainfall is uncommon, the floods caused "a widespread power outage after numerous electricity poles fell", as well as other damage and landslides, municipal spokesman Omar Kachaka told a local television channel.
Rashid al-Alimi, the Riyadh-based president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, called on Yemenis on Friday to mobilise and join the armed forces.
He also offered a future general amnesty to Houthi fighters and affiliates who leave the group starting 26 September.
The military chiefs of staff of Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have finished a meeting in Riyadh to discuss how to respond to the Houthis' ongoing attacks on the kingdom, Ankara said on Friday.
Turkey's defence ministry earlier said its chief of general staff was travelling to Saudi Arabia on Friday to attend the meeting, with Saudi state media also announcing planned military talks but without providing further details.
Later on Friday, Ankara published photographs of the three military officials in uniform, stating that the meeting had taken place, without disclosing where.
The Iran-backed group has escalated its attacks on the kingdom since July, ending a years-long truce and declaring a maritime blockade, hitting Saudi targets and seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast as they seek to stifle Saudi oil exports.
Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until "all of Iran’s conditions are met" by the United States.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
US President Donald Trump said Friday he had discussed the Iran war with visiting Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, following allegations that Beijing has been supporting Tehran.
"We did, we did," Trump said when asked if they had talked about Iran, as he showed Xi around the National Archives in Washington on the last day of the Chinese leader's state visit.
Asked if he thought there would be progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Trump replied: "I think we're going to do great."
China sent around 1,300 shipments of dual-use components suitable for drones and missiles to Iran in the first half of 2026, according to Iranian customs data seen by The Wall Street Journal.
The components included electronics, GPS devices, electric motors, aircraft-engine parts and other items that can support Iran’s drone programs and missile guidance systems.
One notable delivery arrived in Tehran on 17 June, the same day the US and Iran agreed to a 60-day truce.
Two days later, more than a dozen shipments landed carrying more than $6 million worth of parts usable in drones.
Colombia's new far-right US-backed government said on Thursday it had cut diplomatic ties with Iran based on "hemispheric national security" considerations.
It accused the Iranian government of having ties to "narco-terrorist groups that threaten the security of the country," without giving proof of the allegations.
Iran's foreign ministry hit back on Friday, calling the allegations "baseless claims".
Iraq's Najaf airport, a top destination for Shia pilgrims, suspended all Iranian flights on Friday, enforcing US sanctions and leaving travellers scrambling for solutions.
Airport director Hussein Muhanna told AFP that "all flights were halted between Iran and Najaf airport following a directive from the prime minister's office to the governor" of Najaf.
"All Iraqi airports, including in Kurdistan, have enforced the ban," a government source told AFP.
The airport in the holy city of Najaf, south of Baghdad, is a major hub for Iranian flights and their main destination in Iraq.
They mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran's holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran, and patients seeking medical treatment there.
The United Nations' top official for refugees warned on Friday that conditions for long-displaced people in Western Sahara were getting worse and that their humanitarian needs were starkly underfunded.
Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, has been largely controlled by Morocco since 1975, but the United Nations considers it a non-self-governing territory.
Morocco has waged a decades-old conflict with the Algerian-backed Polisario Front, which seeks independence for the Sahrawi people.
"In Western Sahara, displacement has persisted for more than half a century," the UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, himself a former refugee, told the UN Security Council. "Generations of Sahrawi refugees have grown up in Tindouf and camps nearby, facing uncertainty and limited prospects."
The top diplomats of Egypt and Iran met on Friday to discuss resuming peace talks between Tehran and Washington, Egypt's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
The foreign ministers discussed "proposals being put forward to reach an agreement that leads to containing tensions and de-escalation", it said.
“[Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr] Abdelatty also underscored the importance of respecting the security and stability of Gulf states and all nations in the region,” the statement added.
The meeting came after Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi submitted a new seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume peace negotiations with the US.
