articles.title: Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says
Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear programme even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until “all of Iran’s conditions are met” by the United States.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
In a meeting with journalists on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said he hoped a deal with Washington to end the hostilities could be reached before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources.
(Reuters)

articles.title: Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing nuclear weapons, US intelligence warns - report
articles.body:
US intelligence assessments said Saudi Arabia has not ruled out developing a nuclear weapons program, according to classified documents provided to Congress and reviewed by officials who spoke to The Washington Post.
The assessment was included in classified documents submitted to Congress as part of a review of a US-Saudi agreement to expand civilian nuclear cooperation.
The intelligence assessment raised concerns among some US lawmakers over the agreement reached by US President Donald Trump’s administration, which would allow American companies to pursue tens of billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects in Saudi Arabia.
The agreement has also drawn scrutiny because it could eventually allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium to 20%, according to The Washington Post. The deal initially limits enrichment to below 5%, but allows the limit to rise to 20% after an additional study and written agreement.
The Washington Post did note that uranium enriched to 20% is still below weapons-grade levels.
US Senators warn the agreement could give Saudi Arabia the ability to develop a bomb
The agreement is currently subject to a 90-day congressional review period, during which lawmakers can seek to block it.
A group of Democratic senators led by Ed Markey of Massachusetts and Jeff Merkley of Oregon said in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the agreement could give Saudi Arabia the ability to enrich uranium and potentially develop nuclear weapons.
“The Trump administration is departing from precedent, adopting looser restrictions, and caving to Saudi demands,” the senators wrote.
Merkley told The Washington Post that the United States should not rely on assurances from the Saudi government regarding its nuclear intentions. He also questioned why Riyadh would seek the ability to enrich uranium domestically if its nuclear program were intended solely for civilian purposes.
The Saudi government did not respond directly to questions from The Washington Post but referred the newspaper to an earlier statement by Saudi Energy Minister Abdulaziz bin Salman, who said the program would be “peaceful” and developed with “the highest levels of responsibility and transparency.”
The State Department also defended the agreement, telling The Washington Post that the United States “does not and will not support a Saudi nuclear weapon program.”
The department said the agreement would expand nuclear energy cooperation while maintaining what it described as the strongest nonproliferation standards that could be achieved diplomatically.
The intelligence community's assessment was included alongside input from the State Department, according to US officials who spoke to The Washington Post on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified information. The State Department's assessment was described as more confident in the agreement's safeguards and Saudi assurances.
The CIA declined to comment.
Another concern was that the agreement did not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol, which gives the agency broader access to nuclear facilities and research sites.
Twenty nuclear nonproliferation experts, including former IAEA director general Hans Blix, warned in a letter to Congress this week that the inspection arrangements could make it difficult to determine whether Saudi Arabia was secretly developing nuclear weapons at undeclared facilities.
Saudi Arabia will develop a nuclear weapon if Iran does
Concerns over Saudi Arabia's nuclear ambitions have also been linked to comments by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in 2018 that Riyadh would develop a nuclear weapon if Iran did so.
The Trump administration conducted joint Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and in 2026, but Iran's enriched uranium is believed to have survived the attacks under the rubble of the damaged facilities, according to The Washington Post.
The possibility of Saudi Arabia developing nuclear weapons has raised concerns among some US lawmakers that nuclear activity in the kingdom could contribute to a broader regional arms race.
The Trump administration has said the nuclear agreement is intended to strengthen US-Saudi ties and prevent Riyadh from deepening cooperation with countries including Russia and China.
The agreement could also have implications for US efforts to secure Saudi normalization of relations with Israel.
Trump has said normalization remains a requirement for the nuclear deal, although Saudi Arabia has not agreed to establish diplomatic relations with Israel while the Israeli government continues to oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state.

articles.title: Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns
articles.body:
Danish intelligence officials have warned that Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, on Thursday identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it wrote in a report.
"The purpose would be to redirect European resources away from supporting Ukraine and to sow division within NATO, should the alliance fail to agree on a collective response."
The DDIS added that it saw no indications that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a NATO country, although it said it could not rule this out.
Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops, possibly without national insignia, into NATO countries on its border, the DDIS said. However, it said that such a buildup would be difficult to conceal and take several months to prepare.
The new threat assessment joins a chorus of Russia warnings from top European security officials and lawmakers in recent days.
NATO members that border Russia are Finland, Norway and Poland as well as the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Poland's government on Thursday said a blaze at a Starlink ground station in the country was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military.
Poland's deputy prime minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, said it had not yet been established who was responsible for the fire, but "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new doctrine of attack," according to Reuters.
A spokesperson for Russia's embassy in London was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC. The Kremlin has previously denied involvement in similar incidents.
Denmark's intelligence service also warned that Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more attacks against the West and NATO, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past."
These could include major cyberattacks that seriously damage vital societal functions as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, the DDIS said.

articles.title: Iranian President Pezeshkian talks about proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian talks about proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz, says Iran would allow nuclear inspectors
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said there was an "atmosphere of distrust" between Iran and the U.S. when asked whether he would have been willing to meet with President Trump in New York this week, an idea raised by the U.S. leader.
Pezeshkian, during an interview with "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" Friday, suggested that he would need to know "what exactly we want to reach an understanding on," after running through a list of the times the U.S. has attacked Iran while the countries were in the midst of negotiations.
But he also said Iran would "abide by whatever we commit to" if the U.S. accepts the latest Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran's foreign minister offered a proposal this week to reopen the strait after seven days and restart talks with the U.S. as an initial step toward a final nuclear deal. The U.S. has yet to respond to the Iranian proposal, which was announced during the United Nations General Assembly in New York City.
Mr. Trump had expressed openness to meeting with Iranian officials in New York. Although top Trump officials held indirect talks with Iranian officials through mediators, the president himself did not. During his speech to the General Assembly, Mr. Trump said he has a "big decision to make" on whether to cut a deal with Iran or "annihilate" the country. He also predicted that the two sides will not reach an agreement until after the midterms.
Pezeshkian suggested it would be difficult for him to meet face-to-face with Mr. Trump, pointing to an "atmosphere of distrust that has developed between Iran and the United States."
"As long as they don't cease doing what they're imposing on us every day, it's difficult to trust them," he said. "Every day, they increase the sanctions against us. Every day, they threaten us. Every day, they strike us. And they don't honor what they have put in writing. So if they engage in talks, will they actually follow through?"
Brennan asked when Iran expects a response from the United States on its offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart negotiations.
"If this message reaches the president of the United States, or the interviewers and those involved in the discussions, naturally the process will begin from the very day they accept it," he said.
He blamed the U.S. for the collapse of the ceasefire agreement known as the "memorandum of understanding," or MOU, over the summer, after Iran targeted commercial shipping vessels and the U.S. responded by carrying out attacks on Iran.
The U.S. has insisted Iran should not control the waterways entering the Strait of Hormuz, including those that pass Omani territory, or charge tolls for ships that pass through. Iran has demanded that ships seek permission and follow an Iranian-approved shipping route.
"If they operate according to that framework, I think all of us will abide by it," he said of the original U.S.-Iran agreement.
The 60-day ceasefire deal that fell apart in July was designed to buy time for Iran and the U.S. to hold talks on the future of Iran's nuclear program — a thorny issue that both sides have struggled to reach a deal on.
In recent years, Iran has enriched uranium to near weapons-grade levels of purity, and while it denies any interest in building a nuclear weapon, it has refused to give up uranium enrichment altogether.
Mr. Trump has said in the past that Iran must stop enriching uranium — a more hardline stance than the Obama-era nuclear deal that allowed Iran to enrich to a low level, with limits on the size of its program and international inspectors.
Pezeshkian told Brennan Iran would now allow U.N. nuclear inspectors into the country.
"That is absolutely correct," he said.
Brennan pointed out that inspectors from the U.N.'s International Atomic Energy Agency were not given full access when they tried before.
"Will your country allow in weapons inspectors now?" Brennan asked again.
"That is absolutely correct," he responded again, adding, "If they wish to come in and have inspections, we can reach accords and agreements vis-à-vis that specific topic within the negotiations."
At the same time, Pezeshkian claims that Iran is not trying to build a nuclear weapon: "Developing nuclear weapons is haram," he said, using the word forbidden, maintaining that even if some in Iran wanted to build a nuclear weapon, "religiously speaking, they are not allowed to pursue that path."
Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader
Brennan asked Pezeshkian about his communications with Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader, who has not been seen in public since the U.S.-Israeli attack that killed his father, Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, earlier this year.
The Iranian president insisted the new supreme leader has "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges," and said they last met twice, once for over seven hours. He said they were seated "for those many hours" and "changed angles and positions" because they were unaccustomed to being seated for so long.
"From a medical standpoint, he's completely healthy," Pezeshkian said, adding that injuries to his face and legs have recovered. "Hear this from me as a physician, and accept it. He has no issues."
When asked whether Mojtaba Khamenei is advising Pezeshkian on diplomacy, the president explained that there is a team "consisting of six members of various organizations, security forces, parliamentary representatives, government agencies, and they sit and conduct talks, consultations about decision-making processes, and reach any decisions through coordination."
Brennan said it was notable for the Iranians to be in a country they're at war with, when they were in shelters only months earlier.
"We were not in a shelter a few months ago," he said. "How did we manage the country?"
"It's not as if we were in a shelter," Pezeshkian added. "If we were in a shelter, nothing would have gotten done."

articles.title: North Korea’s Ukraine POWs Are Now in South Korea. What Comes Next?
articles.body:
The immediate fate of two North Korean prisoners-of-war captured by Ukrainian forces is no longer in question, but the saga is not yet over.
Ukraine has transferred custody of the pair to South Korea in what was perhaps a predictable outcome given their reported desire not to return to North Korea. However, the circumstances surrounding the disclosure have introduced new political dynamics to the situation. Now, both the South Korean government and the two former soldiers face an unprecedented resettlement process.
Kyiv first announced that it had captured the two North Korean soldiers in January 2025, immediately prompting questions of what would come of the pair. The legal provisions surrounding their eventual disposition were complicated. International rules pointed toward repatriating them with other POWs to Russia. Before the capture happened, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it was his government’s position that all POWs in Ukrainian custody would receive the same treatment.
The two soldiers, however, reportedly expressed fear of repatriation and a desire to defect to South Korea. Given the Kim Jong Un regime’s publicized insistence that soldiers kill themselves rather than be captured, returning to North Korea could have exposed them to reprisals for allowing themselves to be taken into Ukrainian custody. Under the principle of non-refoulement, the potential risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations if the soldiers were ultimately repatriated to North Korea was a necessary consideration.
The South Korean government stepped in early with offers to take the POWs into their custody. With advocacy stretching back to the previous Yoon Suk-yeol administration, there was little doubt over Seoul’s desired outcome for the two individuals.
What is now evident is that the two governments came to a confidential agreement to transfer the custody of the POWs. The handover reportedly took place ahead of the U.N. General Assembly debates, and the two former soldiers are now in South Korean government care. Details of this arrangement first came to light via Zelenskyy himself.
During his speech at the U.N. General Assembly, the Ukrainian president captured international attention when he revealed that Ukraine had transferred custody of the two POWs to South Korea. In the speech, he noted that “these guys are not easy to capture alive,” adding that one of the soldiers, “when he realized he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself.” Zelenskyy’s disclosure came unilaterally and without warning to the South Korean government.
Kyiv’s decision to reveal information despite the confidential arrangement created a diplomatic problem with Seoul, but it also served a clear Ukrainian purpose. Kyiv’s intelligence has repeatedly claimed that the Kremlin is seeking an additional 30,000-50,000 North Korean troops to support a new offensive. Zelenskyy therefore used the U.N. General Assembly debates as a platform to highlight the Kim regime’s continued support for Russia’s war effort and to put North Korea’s military involvement back on the international agenda.
But Zelenskyy’s announcement caused a stir in South Korean domestic politics. Opposition lawmakers immediately chastised the Lee Jae-myung administration for not disclosing the transfer. Some argued that the government was withholding details out of fear of how North Korea may react.
Lee took to social media to push back against this criticism. He said that there was an agreement to keep the transfer confidential, expressing that it was “deeply regrettable” that the Ukraine side released details on the matter. He added that publicly disclosing the successful repatriation could have helped boost approval ratings, but it would not have been right to risk “someone’s life or the national interest” for one’s “own petty benefit.”
There are political reasons why some in the Lee administration may have sought to avoid disclosing information about the POW transfer. The government has been working to rekindle any form of inter-Korean engagement, and some policy groups within Seoul have warned that North Korea could react strongly to the decision.
However, such concerns may be unfounded. North Korean state media has not commented on the POWs since their reported capture, and there are much more significant sticking points between the two Koreas; namely, Pyongyang’s preconditions that Seoul must drop unification and denuclearization as policy objectives. Since Zelenskyy’s announcement, the only reporting from Pyongyang directed toward the South Korean government has been a statement attributed to Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui on a familiar issue: reiterating the Kim regime’s position that denying the reality of North Korea’s nuclear weapon status “is to give up the future.”
Meanwhile, from a security perspective, there are justifiable concerns related to the information disclosure. There have been North Korean assassination attempts against South Korea-based defectors in the past. The most prominent recent example occurred in a 2011 incident in which a North Korean agent attempted to kill prominent defector-turned-activist Park Sang-hak with a poison needle.
The two POWs could therefore present a different security challenge from the average North Korean defector. Their firsthand knowledge of North Korean involvement in the Russia-Ukraine War means that there is a reasonable risk that they could become targets of elimination efforts.
Given the confidential nature of the South Korea-Ukraine agreement, there are few details on what comes next for the two former soldiers. There may have been an understanding that they will remain in custody until the conclusion of the war, or Kyiv may have conceded that South Korea can treat the individuals as they would any other defector. This would affect how long the individuals remain in the government’s custody.
Whatever the length of their initial detention in South Korea, the eventual next step will be resettlement.
Resettlement can be difficult for any defector. New arrivals generally undergo a months-long program at the Hanawon resettlement facility under the Ministry of Unification’s remit, and it includes tasks such as teaching individuals about South Korean customs and courtesies, how to manage bank accounts and finances, and finding employment.
Upon completion of the resettlement process, they are then given relocation assistance to a new residence somewhere in the country. There, they are typically assigned a local officer – either a Ministry of Unification, Korean National Police, or National Intelligence Service (NIS) official – to continue supporting their transition process and to contact in the event of any issues.
The system is different for higher profile or high-risk defectors. They may be former senior North Korean officials like Thae Yong Ho, or figures such as Park Sang-hak who have used their newfound freedom to lead civic movements in protest of the Kim regime. In those cases, the individuals can remain in NIS protective custody until officials determine that it is safe for them to return to public life. Even then, there may be continued protection services.
The two former soldiers transferred from Ukraine will likely fall into that latter category, particularly with the amount of media coverage they have received.
Thus, the arrival of the two North Korean soldiers to South Korea resolves the most immediate question surrounding their fate, but the next steps remain dynamic. The situation has now entered a new phase where South Korean politics will continue to scrutinize the issue as the government works to navigate an unprecedented resettlement process.

articles.title: China, US agree to $30 billion tariff cut, AI dialogue following Xi-Trump summit in Washington
articles.body:
China and the US have agreed to a $30 billion reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement and to launch dialogue on AI, under an eight-point consensus reached during Chinese President Xi Jinping's meeting with US President Donald Trump, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
The two sides recognized the work of their economic teams and endorsed steps including the establishment of a trade council, the tariff-reduction arrangement and an extension of outcomes from earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the ministry said.
The United States and China had earlier agreed to extend by two months a trade truce that was due to expire on November 10, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger trade deal, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday.
Agreement follows three-day summit in Washington
The leaders of the world's two largest economies ended a three-day summit that showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state media Xinhua reported on Saturday.
On artificial intelligence, the two sides agreed to establish a dialogue to discuss the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussion set for November, and to set up a communication channel for AI-related incidents, according to the ministry.
They also agreed to support each other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting and the Group of Twenty summit, with both leaders signaling their intention to attend the gatherings hosted by the other.
On foreign policy, the leaders agreed that Iran should fulfill its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on international waterways, the ministry said. They also recalled that China and the United States fought as allies in World War Two.

articles.title: Air Force Injects $87M into IVEWS F-16 Electronic Warfare Upgrades
articles.body:
The Air Force has invested $87.4 million to upgrade the F-16 Fighting Falcon‘s electronic warfare capabilities, bolstering the fighter’s self-protection against increasingly advanced threats.
Bringing the total program value to $1.92 billion, the move is expected to jump-start fielding by funding low-rate initial production of the AN/ALQ-257 Integrated Viper Electronic Warfare Suite, or IVEWS, which is integrated into the fighter’s airframe.
This money is intended to produce an upgraded Viper for use in the Middle East, as part of an effort pushed by the U.S. military’s Central Command.
Work on the low-rate initial production batch at the company’s Illinois facility is expected to conclude by the end of 2029. The Air Force Lifecycle Management Center, Wright-Patterson, Ohio, oversees the contract.
The Need
The company says the new EW system is sorely needed for the F-16’s future fights.
“You cannot defeat what you cannot see,” said Shalini Gupta, vice president of electronic warfare and targeting at Northrop Grumman, in a statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine. “A modern EW suite is essential for operations in contested airspace. We are producing fully functional, flight-proven systems now. From day one, our customers gain the ability to geolocate threats with a single aircraft, and the confidence that comes with having a U.S. program of record system on board.”
The F-16 has seen a lot of action in Operation Epic Fury, and while its existing capabilities have handled Iranian air defenses and electronic warfare capabilities, peer adversaries such as the Chinese military have more sophisticated means to foil the jet fighter’s aims.
The Air Force issued an urgent operational need statement in 2025 that triggered a congressionally supplied $187 million in its fiscal 2026 reconciliation bill, which sped up system qualification and flight testing.
After CENTCOM’s operational need statement, Northrop and the Air Force made the effort a priority.
“This is one of many efforts to keep our fourth-gen platforms competitive as the adversary advances,” Lt. Gen. Derek France, then-commander of Air Forces Central, said in September 2025 about IVEWS. “That’s the bumper sticker, if you will.”
The recently announced additional $87.4 million LRIP modification fuels the initial production of the Viper suites. Full-rate production of the suites for the full 450-aircraft fleet is scheduled to follow this initial batch.
The initial production tranche for the Air Force was to outfit 72 Block 50 F-16s with IVEWS, with more likely to arrive as production ramps up, the company’s vice president of targeting and survivability Jim Conroy told Air & Space Forces Magazine in a 2025 interview.
Iran operates radar-guided and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) air defense systems. Non-traditional Houthi air defense systems proved a particular challenge for U.S. aircraft, including F-16s, during last year’s Operation Rough Rider against the group in Yemen.
During Operation Epic Fury, the Air Force used its Block 50 F-16s in a suppression of enemy air defenses role and deployed most of its Wild Weasel SEAD F-16 units to support operations against Iran. Those units’ F-16s can carry AGM-88 anti-radiation missiles and are equipped with HARM Targeting System, or HTS, pods—a capability the Air Force’s other fourth-generation fighter, the F-15E Strike Eagle, lacks.
The System
IVEWS is an ultra-wideband, sophisticated EW system capable of radar warning, active jamming, and detecting, identifying, and locating threats, suited for fifth- and sixth-generation aircraft.
It can also conduct single-aircraft autonomous geolocation, meaning one aircraft can find an enemy radar and map a threat while actively using the aircraft’s jammer. Older systems required multiple aircraft to triangulate a radar location and required pilots to shut off jammers when mapping threats.
Under the USAF “Big Iron” software compliance standard, teams will be able to quickly update IVEWS system software files without hardware modifications or grounding the aircraft for days, weeks, or months.
IVEWS began flight tests in 2024 and has undergone more than 550 hours of effective testing across 300 sorties during operational assessments, Northrop Vice President for Mission Systems Mike Minahan said in a July call with reporters.
The system works in conjunction with the AN/AG-83 Scalable Agile Beam Radar. The radar uses an Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) to enable faster target tracking.
As of mid-May, Northrop had delivered 1,000 SABR radars to its F-16 customers. The new radar uses digital tracking as opposed to the legacy AN/APG-66 and AN-APG-68 radars that it is replacing.
IVEWS, the SABR, and the upgraded LITENING LA pod, which gives the aircraft a 50 percent increase in the range of its targeting system, are crucial to keeping the aging F-16 combat-worthy. The pod is also used on the F-15E Strike Eagle, A-10 Thunderbolt II, B-52 Stratofortress, and the Navy F/A-18 Super Hornet.
IVEWS would likely be equipped on possible future Air Force new-build “F-16G” purchases the service will consider, Air & Space Forces Magazine reported.
The LITENING LA, an upgrade from the current LITENING pod, entered flight testing in December, according to Northrop officials.

articles.title: Saudi grand mufti urges troops to sacrifice their lives for ‘complete defeat’ of Houthis
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s top religious authority has issued an unusually forceful appeal to soldiers stationed on the kingdom’s borders, telling them to remain ready to sacrifice their lives in the fight against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis and praying for the group’s “complete defeat.” The message comes amid mounting questions over whether Riyadh could be preparing for a broader military campaign in Yemen after weeks of escalating missile, drone and air attacks.
Grand Mufti Sheikh Saleh bin Fawzan Al-Fawzan said protecting Saudi territory and punishing those who attempt to seize even part of it were among the highest religious duties, “for which lives and souls are sacrificed.” His statement, addressed directly to troops on the front lines, drew heavily on Quranic verses and sayings of the Prophet Muhammad about sacrifice and fighting in defense of God.
“We ask God Almighty to grant you all his support, and to protect our countries and beloved Yemen from all harm,” he said. “We also ask him to bring about the complete defeat of the Houthi group and those who assist and support them.” He urged soldiers to remain constantly prepared, obey Saudi rulers and field commanders and “carry out orders with the utmost precision.”
The rare intervention comes as fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis intensifies sharply. The Saudi-led coalition said Thursday that it intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed toward Taif and the strategically important Red Sea port of Yanbu. The Houthis later claimed missile and drone attacks against what they described as a sensitive target in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. The extent of any damage from the Houthi-claimed strikes has not been independently established.
Saudi Civil Defense has repeatedly issued emergency warnings across parts of the kingdom during the latest escalation, including Jazan, Jeddah, Yanbu, Taif, Mecca and Tabuk. The Houthis have also claimed attacks on Saudi military positions in Jazan, while Saudi Arabia has continued airstrikes against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.
Religion enters an escalating conflict
The grand mufti’s message also appears to reinforce an increasingly religious dimension in Saudi Arabia’s public presentation of the conflict. Saudi state television has aired footage of what authorities said was a Houthi attack on a mosque in the kingdom’s south, while Riyadh has accused the Houthis of attempting to strike Mecca, Islam’s holiest city. The Houthis have rejected Saudi accusations surrounding attacks on holy sites.
Saudi Arabia has fought the Houthis since a Saudi-led coalition intervened in Yemen in 2015, months after the group seized the capital, Sanaa. A 2022 truce largely reduced cross-border fighting, but hostilities have surged again, with the Houthis expanding their position around the Red Sea and Saudi Arabia resuming airstrikes. Recent fighting has increased concern over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Saudi energy infrastructure, including Yanbu, which is particularly important when oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are disrupted.
France has now pledged military assistance to protect Yanbu. President Emmanuel Macron said Paris would send soldiers, radar equipment and defense systems to help safeguard the strategic oil-export site, stressing that the deployment was defensive and was not intended to draw France into the fighting.
Riyadh is also pressing its newer defense partners for support. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan announced an urgent meeting of their military chiefs to discuss assistance to the kingdom under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which provides that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all three. The countries signed the pact in August and have since begun building the mechanisms needed to implement it, although no specific military deployment has yet been announced.
The combination of repeated Houthi attacks, the grand mufti’s appeal to frontline troops and Riyadh’s increasingly urgent search for outside military support has added to speculation over the kingdom’s next move. For now, Saudi Arabia continues to strike Houthi positions from the air while reinforcing defenses at home, as both sides signal that a confrontation once held largely in check could be entering a more dangerous phase.

articles.title: Israel’s October 7 lesson: How a state can survive in a volatile Middle East - opinion
articles.body:
In the Middle East, a state that desires peace cannot assume it will live in peace, and a state that avoids war cannot assume war will avoid it.
Alliances in this region change rapidly. Stable states sit beside fragile states, militias, and ideological groups. The interests of major powers tangle with the conflicts of regional powers. A state may find itself pulled into a confrontation it did not choose, or watch its territory, economy, and infrastructure become a tool for one party to pressure another.
The question of national security therefore goes beyond preventing a war. It concerns stopping danger before it fully forms, discouraging an adversary from exploiting it, and ensuring the state can still function if all safeguards fail and the blow lands.
Israel offers the clearest example of this dynamic, given its location, geography, and the history of conflict around it.
Since its founding, the country has contended with limited strategic depth. The history of confrontation on its borders means a major security failure carries different consequences than the same failure would in states with more territory and greater distance from front lines.
Israel’s security doctrine has historically rested on deterrence, warning, decisiveness, and defense. Prevention later gained a larger role.
The October 7, 2023, Hamas-led massacre did more than add a new element to that doctrine. It exposed the danger of trusting an adversary to remain deterred, and the danger of treating an assessment of intentions as a security guarantee.
It revived an old truth in Israeli thinking: the latitude you grant your enemy today may become tomorrow the danger that catches your state unprepared.
Permanent preparedness or repeated failure
After that day, the entire cost calculus changed. For Israel, the question was no longer a simple tradeoff between high military readiness and a calm period that allows lower spending. It became a choice between the cost of permanent preparedness and the risk of repeating a failure whose consequences could far outweigh the money saved during quiet years.
Deterrence stays essential, intelligence more so, and military readiness cannot drop to a level that would require months to rebuild when a crisis starts. This carries a heavy economic, social, and political price. It has come to be seen as the cost of lowering the chance of surprise, rather than a burden that can be put off indefinitely.
Prevention by definition does not begin after danger strikes or a breach occurs. At that point, the state has already moved from stopping danger to managing its aftermath.
Prevention begins much earlier, before rockets launch and before fighters cross borders. It begins when capability takes shape in weapons stockpiles, smuggling routes, command and funding structures, training sites and positioning areas, and in rocket and drone systems that build up under cover of waiting.
Prevention, in this sense, does not mean unlimited use of force. It means targeting a specific capability that poses an operational danger before it matures into a full threat.
The lessons from Israel’s experience apply elsewhere. The same geopolitical conditions, in varying degrees, impose a similar logic on other states in the region.
The recent Gulf war demonstrated that location, wealth, international ties, and balanced policies offer no complete immunity when the region erupts. Iran targeted Gulf states and their vital economic infrastructure as part of a broader confrontation with the United States and Israel.
The Gulf, in one aspect of this strategy, became an area that could be hurt so that political and economic pain would reach Washington, the West, and global markets.
The lesson is stark. A state can declare it wants no confrontation, open channels for mediation, and maintain relations with opposing parties. That does not force its adversary to read the situation the same way.
If the adversary believes striking it will pressure a larger power or raise the cost of war for others, the state may become a target despite having no role in starting the conflict.
Iran has specifically shown its calculations change when the cost of action becomes tangible, and when it believes the other side can reach its centers of gravity and inflict damage hard to absorb. Deterrence here does not come from good intentions. It comes from a capability the adversary knows exists and must account for in its planning.
Even so, deterrence offers no complete protection. What happens if one rocket gets through defenses and hits a major power station? What if a desalination plant, data center, or port central to trade movement goes offline?
At that moment, another test appears that aircraft and missiles alone cannot settle: the state’s ability to continue after receiving the blow.
Here, the meaning of strength also changes. What matters is not only keeping the adversary from reaching its target, but making the adversary know that hitting the target will not produce the desired result. The more alternatives and backup capacity a state has, the less effective any single blow becomes.
Inflicting damage differs from paralyzing a state. Real preparation starts years before a crisis, with sufficient stockpiles, repair capacity, and institutions that know how to operate when basic services fail.
No matter how strong domestic capacity grows, international alliances remain an important part of the security equation.
Alliances carry weight. They cannot replace domestic capacity, however. An ally may supply weapons and intelligence. It cannot manage a state’s internal crises or restart systems that have broken down inside it.
In this sense, Israel’s experience amounts to more than a special case. It serves as an early testing ground for questions that states across the region have begun to face in their own ways.
The requirement is not to copy Israel. Differences in geography, society, and politics make that pointless. The requirement is to grasp the lesson that its environment forced on it decades ago, and that October 7 brought forcefully back to attention.
Security costs money. Intelligence costs money. Ready armies cost money. Creating alternatives, stockpiles, and redundant vital structures also costs money. Discovering the need for these things after war begins, however, usually proves the costliest option of all.
The Middle East grants its states no permanent guarantees. This is not a call for militarization of the region or for treating war as unavoidable fate. It is a call for understanding the region as it is, not as we wish it were.
The most durable peace requires a state that resists blackmail and paralysis, and whose adversary knows that striking one of its assets will neither break its will nor disable its ability to continue.
This is the doctrine of the survivable state. In a region like ours, a state may not get to choose when the next crisis arrives.
It can decide today, however, whether to enter that crisis counting on it never happening, or prepared for it to happen and able to endure afterward without the adversary robbing it of its capacity to carry on.
The writer is a UAE political analyst and former Federal National Council candidate.

articles.title: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day ceasefire plan, sees renewed bombing after midterms
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire and told aides he expects U.S. bombing of Iran to resume after the November midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing U.S. officials. The reported position comes as Washington and Tehran continue indirect negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and Iran’s nuclear program.
Tehran’s proposal would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear negotiations in exchange for Washington lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, releasing some frozen Iranian assets and easing sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Iran has separately outlined a seven-day roadmap centered on those demands.
Trump has publicly argued that Iran is under severe economic pressure and seeking an agreement that would come after the midterms and dismantle its nuclear program.
Privately, however, he remains skeptical that Tehran would ultimately meet U.S. demands and has told aides that he considers another bombing campaign likely, according to U.S. officials.
The position suggests the conflict, currently suspended between active warfare and a negotiated settlement, could move back toward military confrontation. Officials cautioned, however, that Trump’s approach has shifted repeatedly during the seven-month conflict and could change again in the coming weeks, including after the midterm elections.
Trump reluctant to return to major combat
The scale of any strikes Trump is considering remains unclear.
Officials said he is reluctant to restart major combat operations in part because the United States wants to preserve dwindling stocks of munitions for other possible conflicts.
At the same time, Trump has repeatedly used the threat of large-scale military action to try to break diplomatic deadlocks with Iran. On several occasions he has followed through with strikes, while stopping short of some of his most sweeping threats.
Trump insisted during his speech to the United Nations this week that electoral politics would not determine his policy toward Iran.
“The Republican Party is running, and I’ll be helping them, but I am not running. I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence through the election when it comes to Iran,” he told world leaders during the annual General Assembly in New York. “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump has also urged Republican voters to behave as though he himself were on the ballot in November.
Seven-day plan puts Hormuz at center of talks
Despite Trump’s rejection of the proposal, negotiations between Washington and Tehran are continuing through regional mediators, a U.S. official said.
An American-led effort to keep oil tankers moving through the Strait of Hormuz despite Iranian threats has reduced Washington’s urgency to reach an agreement, according to the official.
Qatar and other regional governments have been trying to revive the negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
During a meeting in Qatar on Sunday, Iran raised the possibility of a seven-day pause in fighting that could lead to an end to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in exchange for the United States lifting its blockade, according to people familiar with the discussions.
Under Tehran’s proposal, Washington would lift the naval blockade, release some frozen Iranian assets and ease sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Iran, in return, would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and begin negotiations over its nuclear program.
The United States has told Iran and regional mediators that Trump has no intention of lifting the maritime blockade, according to officials familiar with the negotiations.
Washington believes that continued economic pressure will eventually push Tehran toward an agreement on terms more favorable to the United States and Arab states in the Persian Gulf.
Tehran divided over how far to compromise
Arab mediators said Iranian diplomats have put forward several proposals aimed at ending the war and have acknowledged the worsening economic crisis inside Iran.
But the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, Iran’s powerful military and economic force, has resisted new formulas for an agreement and has signaled that it is prepared for a prolonged conflict.
The IRGC has effectively dominated decision-making in Iran since the war began in February and wants negotiations to return closer to the preliminary agreement Trump reached with Tehran in June.
That arrangement envisioned sanctions relief for Iranian oil sales, access to frozen Iranian funds and recognition of a role for Tehran in administering traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for reopening the strategic waterway.
For now, Washington is refusing to surrender what it sees as one of its strongest sources of leverage, while Tehran is seeking to revive the concessions contained in the earlier deal. That leaves the two sides still negotiating, but with Trump privately preparing his aides for the possibility that diplomacy could once again give way to airstrikes.

articles.title: Five killed, over 20 injured in overnight strikes as Russia, Ukraine trade blame
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine have traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that killed five people and injured over 20 others.
“Five people were injured in a hostile overnight drone attack. Casualties include one person in Taganrog and four in Azov — among them a child — following the impact of drones on residential buildings,” said Yury Slyusar, governor of Russia’s southern Rostov region, on Telegram on Saturday.
Slyusar said all of those injured had been hospitalised. He claimed that more than 30 drones were downed by air defences over multiple cities in the region, including the city of Rostov-on-Don, as well as over the Azovsky, Myasnikovsky and Neklinovsky districts.
In the city of Azov, falling drones damaged apartment buildings, private homes, industrial facilities, a school, a cultural center and vehicles, Slyusar stated.
Veniamin Kondratyev, governor of the neighboring Krasnodar region, said a drone attack in Seversky district damaged a residential building and caused fires at two industrial facilities in the area.
The operational headquarters of the Krasnodar region later reported that three people were killed and two others injured in the region, adding that the fires at industrial facilities have been extinguished and that about 26,000 residents are currently without electricity.
Ukraine's General Staff claimed that it launched an overnight attack on the Ilsky oil refinery, situated in the Seversky district.
The Russian Defence Ministry claimed it downed 645 Ukrainian drones over 13 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
The ministry further claimed that overnight Russian strikes in Ukraine hit a data centre that “facilitated mobile internet operations and supported Starlink satellite communication systems for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” in the capital Kiev.
It also claimed hitting a port facility, a road bridge, and a logistics centre in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, as well as a dry-cargo vessel “transporting military supplies” in the Black Sea.
Strikes in Ukraine
In the Ukrainian capital, the Kiev City Military Administration said a drone struck between a five-story residential building and a commercial establishment in the city’s Solomianskyi district, where an office building was also damaged.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been injured, adding that search and rescue efforts in the area were ongoing.
He later said a fire broke out near warehouse buildings in the Darnytskyi district, while another fire occurred at a store after a drone fell on the territory of a shopping centre in the Sviatoshynskyi district.
In the broader Kiev region, two people were injured in the Boryspil district, where a fire broke out in a warehouse building, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service.
Meanwhile, Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said a “massive” attack took place on the region’s civilian infrastructure, damaging the facades and windows of more than 10 private homes and apartment buildings, a hotel and restaurant complex, and administrative buildings at a business facility in the southern part of the region.
Elsewhere, in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, two people were killed and seven others injured in the regional capital, according to local authorities.
"We ask (US) President (Donald) Trump to implement the Lindsey Graham Act against Russia and everyone who props up its war financially," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X, commenting on the overnight strikes. He further called on European leaders to impose additional sanctions on Moscow.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defences shot down 134 of 173 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the ongoing war.
Moscow and Kiev have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centres, ports and energy infrastructure.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining the strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: The Fight to Rein In AI Is Dividing Washington
articles.body:
Both Senator Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Senator Martin Heinrich (D-New Mexico) went to the podium on the Senate floor last week with a similar message: AI labs should pay for the energy costs associated with their ballooning data-center footprint, rather than everyday Americans.
But when Husted requested a speedy passage of the Ratepayer Protection Act—a bill that would have required states to consider forcing companies that consume a lot of energy to pay for the related costs—Heinrich blocked the move. He said the legislation was inadequate because it relied on voluntary commitments from states and proposed his own bill as an alternative.
He had another incentive to block Husted’s request: The Ratepayer Protection Act, which earlier this month passed the House 417-3, would have given the Ohio senator a victory amid a competitive reelection campaign. Husted has faced an onslaught of negative ads over the role he played as lieutenant governor in expanding data centers across the state.
“The Ratepayer Protection Act might make a lot of politicians feel good, but it won’t do anything to actually force data centers to pay their fair share,” Heinrich said in a statement. “Democrats are ready for a real solution, and I think that’s exactly what Americans want to see, too.” Husted blamed Democrats for giving big tech companies “a free pass” while Americans’ electric bills continue to rise.
That kind of partisan arm wrestling is likely just a prelude to the bigger fights ahead if Congress gets serious about passing AI legislation.
Democrats, and some Republicans, have proposed hundreds of AI-related bills as Americans become increasingly worried about the ways AI companies may disrupt the job market, raise their energy bills, and even wipe out humanity. Lawmakers’ pro-regulation rhetoric in Washington reached new heights this month after the resignation of former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon gained worldwide attention for posting on X that frontier AI labs were “gambling with our lives.” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei responded with calls for an industry slowdown and government intervention to coordinate global safety standards.
With less than two months before midterms, some members of Congress are feverishly introducing even more AI bills, including at least seven since Coxon’s resignation alone. Other lawmakers are urging their colleagues and congressional leadership to quickly bring measures already on the table for a vote. Democrats, meanwhile, have taken aim at the Trump administration, urging Trump to discuss AI safety with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
“The mood right now, at least in Congress, is very reactive—and I don't mean that in a good way,” said Suresh Venkatasubramanian, director of Brown University’s Center for Technological Responsibility, Reimagination, and Redesign. “They're trying to push legislation that seems to address what appears to be a problem coming from the [public] narrative but that doesn't always necessarily lead to good policy overall.”
In the short term, tech policy watchers have little hope that Congress will pass a major AI safety bill, especially with a limited number of working days left this year. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana ) has rebuffed some Democrats’ calls to end their recess early to focus on an AI bill. Meanwhile, House Energy and Commerce Committee Chairman Brett Guthrie (R–Kentucky), whose committee would review many of the proposed bills, told Politico at an event that the group probably wouldn’t advance a major bill until next year.
But even with a longer timeline, lawmakers may struggle to turn their rhetoric into action. 
Lawmakers will have to overcome deep differences in their views about how dangerous superintelligent AI systems are to the American people and which AI-related risks merit the most attention. Even if lawmakers coalesce around one AI problem, it may be hard for them to settle on the right mitigation strategy quickly enough to keep up with the pace of AI advancements. And if Democrats take over even one chamber after the midterms next month, legislative debates could end up being even more mired in partisan disputes. They would still have to negotiate with Trump, who has largely dismissed the most catastrophic risks of AI as conspiratorial and resisted calls for more regulation. 
When AI companies are “begging for pacing, or some way for them to pace, and they're turning to the government to help them do that, it really does require the government to act,” said Riki Parikh, a policy director for The Alliance for Secure AI, a bipartisan advocacy group that supports AI regulations. “I just don't know if the dynamics in D.C. will allow for that over the next two years,” he added. “We might not have two years to wait.”
Certain lawmakers have sought to address some of the most extreme risks posed by general-purpose AI models, such as the possibility that these systems could eventually be used to create a new pathogen that sets off a global pandemic, carry out a cyberattack on critical infrastructure, or build biological or radiological weapons. Those worries took on a new sense of urgency in July when OpenAI announced that a group of AI agents went rogue during a cybersecurity test and hacked into a separate company, Hugging Face.
Several of their proposals call for AI labs to submit their models or safety practices for review by independent investigators. Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-California) and Lori Trahan (D-Massachusetts), along with three other lawmakers, have proposed the FRONTIER Act, which requires large AI developers to submit reports about safety incidents, information on the potential catastrophic threats of their models, and their planned mitigations to the Department of Commerce and state attorneys general. The bill calls for independent investigators to review companies’ safety plans, and would authorize the Commerce Department to bar the release of a model if it poses an imminent catastrophic risk.
The idea for independent testing has support within the tech industry. Leading the Future, a PAC that has received money from OpenAI president Greg Brockman, has signaled support for the FRONTIER Act. Amodei, the Anthropic CEO, has said he plans to embed investigators from AI-monitoring nonprofit METR, which officially reviewed OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident, to verify the company’s safety practices.
But the political limits of that approach soon became evident. After Amodei’s announcement, METR faced scrutiny from the right over its ties with effective altruism, a philosophical movement focused on using evidence and reason to determine how to do the most good. The New York Post called the group the “Woke Wizards of AI,” as writers there drew connections between effective altruism, METR, and Anthropic. METR’s president later defended the group on X, arguing it doesn’t take money from frontier AI labs and makes an effort to hire people with diverse viewpoints.
Another issue that has already slowed down negotiations on Capitol Hill is the question of whether a federal AI bill should override state laws—a legislative approach embraced by many Republicans and the Trump White House.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minnesota) have discussed proposing a bill that would expose frontier AI labs to legal liability if they don’t adequately mitigate catastrophic risks of their systems, according to a person familiar with the matter. But as news surfaced that their measure may also preempt some state laws, they appeared to face pushback from Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington), ranking member of the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee. “I welcome the urgency. But the answer is not a weak federal standard that becomes a backdoor for wiping out stronger state protections,” she posted on X.
So far, most lawmakers have stopped short of backing a proposal from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) to ban superintelligent artificial intelligence, which the lawmakers define as AI “that exceeds human cognitive performance.” Sanders and Casar also propose pausing the development of advanced AI models until the government sets up the Department of Artificial Intelligence to oversee their safety. Critics say passing that kind of law would only allow Chinese tech companies to make gains in the AI race—a more dangerous prospect in the end.
One policy area where there has been more progress is lawmakers’ attempts to restrict China’s access to advanced American chips, with the goal of preserving the country’s technological lead in the AI race. The Chip Security Act—which requires advanced chips to include a mechanism for verifying their location if they have fallen into the wrong hands—may be folded into an upcoming defense spending bill, the National Defense Authorization Act, said Rep. Bill Foster (D-Illinois).
“It does no good at all if we have all kinds of [AI] rules in the United States or even in the free democracies of the world, and then these [chips] all get smuggled into China, into Russia, [and] into North Korea,” said Foster.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York) and other key Democrats earlier this week urged Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) to bring the Chip Security Act, along with two other bills designed to address tech exports to China, to the floor for a vote.
Still, even those bills face political challenges. Industry critics argue that restricting the exports of American tech only encourages China to invest in its own chips. The defense spending bill has been stalled in the Senate since Democrats blocked its advancement in July in protest of Trump’s handling of the Iranian war.
Perhaps the most likely measure for Congress to address after the midterms would be a bill that tackles energy costs stemming from AI companies’ data centers. “There isn't agreement on what else would be valuable to do right now,” said Bruce Mehlman, a veteran lobbyist whose bipartisan firm represents several tech companies.
“Everybody's concerned about safety, but nobody knows what the concern should turn into legislatively.”

articles.title: Iran submits seven-day Hormuz plan; Yemen forces advance in Taiz
articles.body:
Hello and welcome to today's coverage of the Middle East and beyond. Here is the latest:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has put forward a seven-day proposal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, adding during a visit to New York that Tehran is ready to implement the plan as soon as Washington agrees to it.
In Yemen, government forces advance towards the Taiz and Lahaj governorates, coinciding with a call for "mobilisation" to confront Houthi troops. At least 13 Houthi militants have been killed and dozens others injured in the past 24 hours of fighting, according to Aden-based government figures.
US actor Adam Brody said he wants a "free Palestine" on Friday while promoting his show Nobody Wants This, after several Hollywood actors were arrested during a protest against the arrival of Israel's ICC fugitive Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
In an interview with GQ, Brody, known for his breakout role in the series The O.C., said he wants to noted as being among those who believe a genocide is occurring in Gaza.
“Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine,” Brody said when asked if he would like to speak about the topic.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran's new plan to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was coordinated with supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, state media reported Saturday, quoting an interview with US media.
Pezeshkian also told broadcaster CBS that the Islamic republic would fulfil its obligations were the United States to agree to the proposal, according to excerpts released by state news agency IRNA.
The strait is crucial for the world's oil supply and central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which remains deadlocked after nearly seven months.
"Coordination with the leader of the revolution (the supreme leader)... has been carried out," Pezeshkian said.
"If the US accepts it and fulfils its obligations, we will do the same, and there will be no issue in this regard," he added.
Pezeshkian said that a six-member team in Iran has been meeting for discussions and has "the authority to make decisions".
This team includes representatives from "various organisations and bodies, including the military, the parliament and the government".
Ireland delays presser amid pressure to boycott Israel games
The Ireland team’s press conference the day before the first of its Nations League games against Israel has been delayed as pressure to boycott the matches grows.
Journalists in Debrecen, Hungary — where Israel’s "home" game is to be played Sunday — were left waiting Saturday after being told the press conference was being pushed back until after training. That was 15 minutes before it was supposed to begin.
Training was also delayed, however, with Irish broadcaster RTÉ reporting the players were still in their hotel when it was supposed to begin.
The team has been coming under increasing pressure in Ireland, where affinity with Palestinians is strong, to boycott the two games — the first on Sunday and the second, Ireland’s “home” game, in Backa Topola, Serbia on Oct. 4.
Ireland midfielder Jason Knight said after Thursday’s 1-0 loss in Kosovo that the players were in a difficult situation and that he didn’t think the matches should be going ahead.
The Iraqi government said Saturday it was holding talks with the United States to secure an exemption from the ban on Iranian airlines, which has disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.
All Iraqi airports enforced the ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport of the holy city of Najaf, the main destination for Iranian flights to Iraq.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians," it added.
Israeli forces and military vehicles are stationed by Birzeit University north of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to Palestinian media.
The university, meanwhile, has condemned the Israeli military raid, claiming "intimidation" of students during final exams is "flagrant and explicit violation" of conventions and laws that protect education.
Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a missile fired by Houthis
Saudi Arabia's military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, claimed early Saturday that a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen was intercepted and destroyed.
Al-Maliki said the missile was fired toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.
There was no immediate statement of responsibility, though it can take days for the Houthis to issue one.
A regional body representing Arab Gulf states, the Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the latest Houthi attacks as a "grave escalation and threat to regional security" and urged the international community to respond.
A bus overturns in central Iran, killing 11 and injuring 24
A passenger bus overturned in Iran, killing 11 people and injuring 24 others, state television reported Saturday.
The crash occurred on the Saveh-Hamedan freeway in central Markazi province. Provincial traffic police said driver fatigue and drowsiness caused the crash.
Authorities did not immediately say where the bus was headed.
Iran has one of the world’s worst traffic safety records. Crashes kill more than 17,000 people a year. Experts blame the high toll on unsafe vehicles, widespread disregard for traffic regulations and inadequate emergency services.
Earlier this month, a fuel tanker crashed into other vehicles and exploded near the western city of Sanandaj, killing 11 people and injuring seven others.
Libya's NOC shuts Zawiya refinery due to pipeline closure
Libya's National Oil Corporation said on Saturday it has shut down one of the refining units at the Zawiya refinery due to the continued forced closure of the Sharara crude pipeline valve by armed groups belonging to the Petroleum Facilities Guard.
The corporation warned that ongoing disruptions to the flow of crude could directly impact state oil revenue, increase fuel import costs and harm the national economy.
The closure has reduced cumulative production at the Sharara field by 942,376 barrels over five days through Friday, causing direct financial losses of about $95 million, the NOC said.
Lost output on Friday alone totalled 222,014 barrels, according to NOC.

articles.title: Zelenskyy discusses production of interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shaheds and data centre protection
articles.body:
Zelenskyy discusses production of interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shaheds and data centre protection
The Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief discussed the results of tests of interceptors against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones on 25 September.
Source: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote: "The teams working on interceptions delivered reports on the shoot-down rate and their experience. We identified the main capabilities that can strengthen our defence. We are accelerating production. There are also new decisions on establishing in Ukraine the production of different types of jet engines."
Details: Zelenskyy also reported on a briefing by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine on Russia's technological plans for 2027, including the systems Russia is counting on, its production capabilities, and supply chains delivering components to Russia.
Quote: "We are adjusting our countermeasures in line with these threats. A priority task for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine and our entire diplomatic service is securing new sanctions packages from our partners, specifically targeting the shadow networks the Russians use to sustain the production of drones and missiles, especially ballistic missiles."
Details: The president said that additional decisions have been made to protect data centre infrastructure and ensure its uninterrupted operation, as well as that of other facilities that are critical to the communications sector.
Background:
- One of Kyiv's data centres housing the core equipment of the Utels internet service provider was damaged in a Russian attack on 23 September.
- A Datagroup data centre was damaged in a Russian attack on 25 September.
