articles.title: EXPLAINER- How panda diplomacy became part of US-China ties
articles.body:
- Chinese President Xi Jinping says 2 pandas will arrive in Atlanta ‘in a few days,’ continuing a diplomatic tradition closely associated with Nixon’s 1972 China visit
- Once goodwill gifts, pandas now travel under conservation agreements that support research, breeding and habitat protection
-  Atlanta’s incoming pair will bring US giant panda population to 6, as renewed loans offer a sign of cooperation amid wider tensions
Two giant pandas heading from China to Atlanta will join a diplomatic tradition that has linked American zoos and Chinese leaders for more than eight decades.
“In a few days, two pandas – Ping Ping and Fu Shuang – will come to their new home in Zoo Atlanta and meet with the American people,” Chinese President Xi Jinping announced Thursday before talks with US President Donald Trump at the White House.
"The giant panda has been an envoy of friendship between the Chinese and Americans," he added, giving a familiar symbol of cooperation a place alongside much-anticipated discussions of trade, geopolitics and technology competition.
The pandas’ destination was already known. Zoo Atlanta announced the agreement in April, identifying Ping Ping as a male and Fu Shuang as a female, both born at China’s Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.
Xi’s remarks supplied the arrival timeframe.
But how did these furry, bamboo-eating bears become symbols of US-China diplomacy? 
How it started
China’s use of pandas as diplomatic gifts predates the establishment of the People’s Republic in 1949.
Some accounts trace panda diplomacy back to the seventh century, when Empress Wu Zetian reportedly sent pandas to Japan during the Tang dynasty.
The practice reemerged in the 20th century.
In 1941, two young pandas, Pan-dee and Pan-dah, arrived at New York’s Bronx Zoo as gifts from Madame Chiang Kai-shek, China’s first lady, thanking Americans for aid to China during its war with Japan, according to the Wildlife Conservation Society’s archives.
The animals were initially thought to be a breeding pair, but both turned out to be female.
In the following decades, the People’s Republic sent pandas to friendly countries, including the Soviet Union and North Korea.
The animals offered China an unusual diplomatic advantage in that wild giant pandas live only in China, making access to them a distinctive gesture of goodwill.
Their appeal also extended beyond government officials. A panda could draw crowds to a zoo and generate public interest in a country that many visitors knew little about. 
The 1972 breakthrough
The best-known episode in US-China panda diplomacy followed President Richard Nixon’s visit to China in February 1972.
The visit helped end more than two decades of estrangement between Washington and Beijing, although formal diplomatic relations were not established until 1979.
During the visit, Nixon’s wife, first lady Pat, mentioned that she liked pandas after seeing them at a Beijing zoo.
Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai responded by offering two pandas to the American people.
Ling-Ling and Hsing-Hsing arrived at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington and were an instant sensation. More than 20,000 people came on the first day, and the following Sunday about 75,000 visitors formed a line a quarter-mile long.
The US reciprocated with a pair of musk oxen, Milton and Matilda.
The musk oxen had a rougher start. Time magazine reported they suffered "culture shock," with runny noses and hair loss, though they eventually recovered. 
From gifts to conservation loans
China moved away from giving pandas outright in the 1980s, turning instead to loans. Over time, long-term conservation and research agreements became the basis for overseas placements.
Such arrangements commonly run for about 10 years and can involve annual payments of around $1 million per pair. Under modern loan agreements, the pandas and their offspring remain Chinese property.
The shift to loans gave panda diplomacy a stronger conservation focus, with zoos contributing funding and expertise to breeding, research and habitat protection.
The US Fish and Wildlife Service listed the species as endangered in 1984 and adopted a conservation-focused panda permit policy in 1998, requiring all panda imports to directly benefit the conservation of pandas in the wild rather than serving short-term commercial exhibition.
The arrangement has been productive. US zoos have successfully raised 17 giant panda cubs – six in San Diego, four in Washington and seven in Atlanta – according to Chinese state media.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature reclassified giant pandas from endangered to vulnerable in 2016, citing a 17% population increase over the decade to 2014, when a nationwide census counted 1,864 in the wild in China, according to the World Wildlife Fund. 
What do panda movements tell us?
Panda arrivals and departures often attract attention far beyond the zoos involved.
As US-China relations deteriorated in recent years, the departure of pandas from American zoos became a particularly visible symbol of the tensions.
In November 2023, the Smithsonian’s National Zoo returned its three pandas to China as their loan agreement expired, leaving Zoo Atlanta as the only US zoo housing giant pandas.
Later that month, after meeting then-President Joe Biden in California, Xi said China was ready to continue panda conservation cooperation with the US – a gesture of goodwill amid efforts to stabilize relations.
A new pair arrived in San Diego in June 2024, before Atlanta’s four pandas departed that October. Another pair arrived in Washington later the same month.
Four giant pandas are currently in the US. Atlanta’s incoming pair would bring the total to six, compared with a historical peak of 15 reported by CNN. 
Atlanta’s next chapter
Zoo Atlanta’s original panda partnership began in 1999 and lasted 25 years. Its pandas produced seven cubs during that period.
The return of its four remaining bears in October 2024 closed that chapter, but the new agreement announced in April opened another.
For Atlanta, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang will restore a major attraction and renew a research partnership. For Beijing, their arrival offers another opportunity to present cooperation with the US through animals that have long drawn American crowds.
Their arrival will not settle disputes over tariffs or AI regulation. But the two bears will offer an adorable reminder that Washington and Beijing still have room for friendship.

articles.title: Iran war squeezes Iraq’s economy as oil revenues fall and prices rise
articles.body:
Iran war squeezes Iraq’s economy as oil revenues fall and prices rise
Disrupted oil exports, costlier imports, and a weaker dinar expose Iraq’s economic dependence on oil, foreign goods.
Iraq is a state heavily dependent on imports, from food and medicines to appliances, as well as raw materials for its industries. Its one big export is oil, but it sits on such a huge supply of the natural resource that revenues from the sale of oil abroad offset the imports and ensured that the country had a positive trade surplus.
Things have changed, however, since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran in late February, and the subsequent end to the free flow of trade through the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the country’s trade with the rest of the world passed. Now, Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has described the country as “facing extraordinary economic challenges”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Netanyahu’s UN belligerence wins cheers at home as world walks out
- list 2 of 3The Trump-Xi summit exposes a US disadvantage in the Global South
- list 3 of 3UAE bars Iranian airlines as US sanctions squeeze Iran’s aviation sector
Al-Zaidi said earlier this week that Iraq had lost about $60bn in oil revenues as a result of the war, the result of being, for a period, unable to export about 90 percent of its oil through its usual Gulf routes, which have become central to negotiations between Washington and Tehran, with the latter linking free passage through the strait to an easing of US pressure and the lifting of a blockade on Iranian ports.
That’s a massive blow to Iraq: oil revenues account for more than 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget.
The disruption to shipping routes has also affected supply chains, increasing transport times and costs for Iraqi businesses and consumers, in addition to reducing imports.
One supermarket owner in Baghdad, Alaa-Eddin Sulaibi, estimated that the percentage of imported goods sold at his store was now 70 percent, down from 90 percent before the war started.
“We have no choice but to sell local products, even if they are not of the same quality as imported ones,” he said.
He added that the price of the imported goods had risen by between 25 and 30 percent.
“The reasons [for the price increase] extend beyond disruptions in the Gulf, but also longer delivery times for goods arriving from China, and higher fuel and transportation costs, particularly for trade with Turkiye,” he said.
Several merchants who spoke to Al Jazeera said goods imported from China were now facing significant delays, in some cases taking up to three months to arrive because of the increase in transportation costs as a result of importers being forced to take more circuitous routes to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, or being delayed at the maritime chokepoint.
Dollar rises against Iraqi dinar
The crisis has put pressure on the Iraqi dinar, which has dropped against the US dollar, in a development that has triggered concern among Iraqis.
The dollar rose to about 1,600 Iraqi dinars on the parallel market last week, before easing to about 1,575 this week. Prior to the war, it had been about 1,540 Iraqi dinars to the dollar.
The widening gap between the official exchange rate – approximately 1,300 dinars to the dollar – and the parallel market rate has also created uncertainty for businesses and added to the financial burden on consumers. The official market rate is largely not available to everyday people, and the divergence in rates allows for some businesses to obtain dollars at the cheaper official rate, while others are forced to use the parallel market and pay more.
At the same time, the Iraqi government is also dealing with concerns about the availability and transfer of dollars that Baghdad receives through arrangements linked to its oil revenues.
Following the fall of the regime of President Saddam Hussein after the 2003 US invasion of Iraq, the country’s oil revenues were placed in a special account in the US, with money then transferred to Baghdad. This transfer is renewed annually by the US president, with the stated purpose of safeguarding Iraq’s financial resources. But the system also gives Washington a large degree of oversight over the flow of dollars from the account to Iraq.
In April, the Trump administration began halting the shipment of physical cash from the account to Iraq, releasing only electronic dollar transfers, with some reporting indicating that the halt in physical cash transfers was linked to pressure over the activities of Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
Some physical cash shipments resumed in July, but the US has also accused several private Iraqi banks of being involved in large-scale dollar smuggling operations to Iran.
Local reports have suggested that the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) is facing difficulties supplying commercial banks with sufficient dollars, particularly for financing imports, potentially leading to higher prices in local markets.
The CBI has denied that it is facing a shortage, saying in a statement on Saturday that it “has sufficient foreign reserves to meet all demands for foreign currency”, adding that included “financing foreign trade”.
The central bank blamed the rise in the parallel market dollar exchange rate on “speculation, expectations, and the misuse of regional geopolitical conditions by certain parties seeking to disrupt Iraq’s economic and financial stability”.
‘Deep imbalances’ in the economy
The pressure on Iraq’s finances is nevertheless intensifying as the war continues and oil revenues fall.
Mudher Mohammed Salih, the Iraqi prime minister’s financial adviser, said in a television interview this week that the CBI’s foreign reserves had fallen from about $106bn before the war began, to roughly $80bn by late August.
Economists say the crisis has exposed longstanding structural weaknesses in Iraq’s economy, particularly its dependence on oil revenues and imported goods.
“This crisis has revealed the deep imbalances within the structure of the Iraqi economy, most notably the absence of safeguards capable of protecting the economy during times of turmoil,” Ziad al-Hashimi, a PhD researcher in international economics at Anglia Ruskin University, told Al Jazeera.
“The crisis has also shown that the Iraqi government lacks genuine solutions or effective measures that could bring about the kind of structural change needed to overcome the situation,” he added.
Al-Hashimi said that the government’s immediate options were limited.
“All the Iraqi government can do are short-term measures that may have only limited the impact in the coming period, such as resorting to borrowing, which is not a genuine solution,” he said. “Real solutions require a long time before results can be seen. They include diversifying Iraq’s oil export markets abroad, managing public spending in a more systematic way to avoid unnecessary expenditures, and continuing efforts to combat corruption.”

articles.title: the runway tells you where to look: 10 fashion shows that rewrote the catwalk
articles.body:
the path of the runway rewritten
Fashion shows typically begin with a straightforward diagram. Models move along a prescribed path, its edges lined with spectators, and everyone knows where to look. In general this basic layout has remained consistent across time. Yet some of the strongest runway sets begin by disturbing that diagram.
Across four decades, designers and scenographers have buried the catwalk beneath the floor, broken it into a grid, or removed the act of walking all together. In these shows, set design shapes much more than just a decorative backdrop. It determines when a model appears and how long they stay visible. It can even determine whether two viewers sitting a few feet apart experience the same sequence. During this season of fashion weeks, we return to ten examples where the runway itself became part of the choreography.
thierry mugler turns the catwalk into an arena
For Thierry Mugler’s fall 1984 show at Le Zénith in Paris, the runway unfolded through the concert venue like a pair of wings. It was one of the first examples of a runway show dreaming beyond the quiet, standard setup. More than 6,000 people filled the room, including paying members of the public, pushing the fashion show beyond the scale of the usual industry presentation. Models could appear at different points across the extended stage, and the audience watched from a wide field instead of a narrow strip beside the garments.
The plan suited Mugler’s theatrical language, but its effect was spatial first. Distance became part of the show. A figure could register as a silhouette from across the arena before moving closer into view, while the runway reached outward toward spectators instead of holding them along one straight edge. The traditional catwalk had been stretched into something closer to a diagram for a crowd.
Thierry Mugler Fall/Winter 1984, Paris | image © Paul van Riel / HH
maison martin margiela shares the runway with its audience
Maison Martin Margiela’s spring/summer 1990 show, presented in fall 1989, moved fashion onto a playground in Paris’s 20th arrondissement. Local children sat along the dirt paths, then began moving among the models as the show continued. The route never hardened into a polished runway. It remained part of the ground everyone was already occupying.
The photographs are completely changed because of that looseness. Models pass close to seated guests, children enter the frame, and the edge between watcher and participant keeps shifting. The runway becomes shared territory. Instead of a protected corridor cut through an audience, Margiela works with a path that can be crossed, crowded, and briefly taken over.
Martin Margiela Spring/Summer 1990, Paris | image © Jean-Claude Coutausse
viktor & rolf stop the runway entirely
Viktor & Rolf pushed the idea in another direction for their fall 1999 couture collection, Russian Doll. Maggie Rizer stood on a rotating platform while Viktor Horsting and Rolf Snoeren dressed her layer by layer, building the collection onto a single body. There was no procession of models moving past the audience. The audience kept returning its gaze to the same point.
The rotating platform turns the usual relationship between clothing and movement inside out. Rizer stays almost fixed while the silhouette expands around her, and the show advances through accumulation instead of distance. The catwalk has effectively collapsed into a circle a few feet wide.
Viktor & Rolf, Russian Doll, Fall/Winter 1999–2000 | video still
alexander mcqueen turns the gaze back on the room
Alexander McQueen’s spring/summer 2001 show, Voss, begins before a model appears. Guests sit around a huge two-way mirrored box and see their own reflections staring back at them. Once the lights shift, the interior becomes visible from outside, while the models inside remain unable to see the audience.
McQueen takes the separation already built into a runway and makes it physical. The model route is contained inside the box, the spectators stay outside it, and the glass controls who gets to see whom. The audience moves from watching itself to observing bodies that cannot return the gaze. Few runway designs make the mechanics of spectatorship so visible.
Alexander McQueen, Voss, Spring/Summer 2001 | image courtesy Alexander McQueen
prada breaks the front row into a field
For Prada men’s spring/summer 2012, AMO treated seating and catwalk as a single plan. Six hundred guests sat on individual blue foam blocks spaced across a 1.5-by-1.5-meter grid, while models followed several choreographed routes through the gaps. Artificial grass covered the floor, turning the hall into a strangely ordered field.
There is no single runway edge to claim. A model might pass directly beside one spectator, then turn through the grid and move toward another. From above, the set reads almost like graph paper filled with people. At eye level, it creates a sequence of brief encounters. The audience is no longer arranged around the route. It helps form the route.
Prada, Field, Men’s Spring/Summer 2012, set design by OMA / AMO, Prada Fondazione, Milan © OMA | image by Agostino Osio
anya hindmarch hides a spiral beneath the floor
At first glance, Anya Hindmarch’s spring/summer 2017 set looked almost empty. A white circular platform sat in the Royal Horticultural Halls in London. When the show began, the platform lifted to reveal a sunken amphitheater and a spiral path beneath it, with a model ascending through the newly opened center. Above, a circular canopy rotated and tilted as the show progressed.
The surprise works because the runway begins as concealed architecture. Its route appears only once the floor moves, turning an apparently flat stage into a section of ramps and levels. Models circle upward through the space, and spectators read their movement across depth as well as distance. The runway is discovered during the show.
Anya Hindmarch, Circulus, Spring/Summer 2017 | image © Neil Mason
dior puts the runway itself in motion
For Dior Men’s fall 2019 show, Kim Jones replaced the conventional catwalk with a 76-meter moving walkway inside a dark box. The models stood still as the belt carried them past the audience, posed almost like figures in a long moving frieze. Jones linked the format to couture salon presentations, where clothing could be observed on relatively stationary bodies.
It is a small reversal with a strange effect. Walking, usually the basic action of a runway, disappears. The floor controls speed and direction instead, sending each look past the same line of viewers at an even pace. The model becomes stationary and the architecture takes over the choreography.
Dior Men’s, Fall/Winter 2019-2020 | video still
balenciaga winds the audience into a double spiral
Balenciaga’s spring/summer 2020 show filled a 2,000-square-meter room with around 500 seats arranged as an elliptical double spiral. Guests sat in a single row that climbed across five levels, all inside a field of saturated blue conceived in reference to a parliamentary chamber. The corridors created by that seating system became the catwalk.
The spiral removes the easy distinction between runway center and audience edge. Spectators face across the room toward one another, while models wind through the same geometry at changing distances. A person several turns away can enter your sightline long before reaching your section. The show becomes something seen across layers of other spectators.
Balenciaga Spring/Summer 2020, set design by SUB | image © Boris Camaca
dior opens the floor beneath the entire cast
Dior Men’s summer 2024 presentation initially offered a broad field of polished metal tiles. Then 51 panels slid open in a three-by-seventeen grid and the full cast rose from beneath the runway on individual lifts. For a few seconds, the collection appeared all at once across the floor before the models began moving through the show.
The entrance usually sits at the end of a runway, somewhere backstage and outside the audience’s view. Here, every point on the floor becomes an entrance. The first image is spatial as much as sartorial: 51 bodies distributed across a precise grid, each occupying a position that had appeared empty seconds earlier.
Dior Men’s summer 2024, set design by Villa Eugénie | image © Adrien Dirand
willo perron sends chanel across two crossing ramps
For Chanel’s spring/summer 2025 haute couture show, Willo Perron laid two broad curving ramps through the Grand Palais. Together they traced Chanel’s double C into a figure-eight path, with the walkways rising and crossing over one another like bridges. The runway became a continuous loop with models moving through changing heights and directions.
Seen from above, the structure reads immediately as geometry. From a seat beside it, that geometry becomes circulation. One model climbs while another passes through a different section of the curve, and the crossing ramps create views above and across the audience’s usual eye line. Perron turns the catwalk from a strip of floor into a route with elevation and overlap.
Chanel Spring/Summer 2025, set design by Willo Perron | image courtesy Chanel
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership with SolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. Discover more stories that turn onlookers into participants, alter perception and disrupt the everyday here.

articles.title: Culture Minister goes to Russia to advance joint cultural programs
articles.body:
Culture Minister goes to Russia to advance joint cultural programs
TEHRAN – The Minister of Culture and Islamic Guidance Seyyed Abbas Salehi has traveled to Russia to attend the 12th International Forum of United Cultures and advance joint cultural programs between Iran and Russia.
The trip began in St. Petersburg and will continue with a meeting of the two countries’ joint cultural committee and the opening of Iran’s Cultural Week in four Russian cities, ISNA reported.
Salehi arrived in Russia on Thursday, and after a brief stop in Moscow, traveled to St. Petersburg to attend the 12th International Forum of United Cultures. Held under the slogan “United Cultures, Common Values,” the event brings together senior officials and prominent figures from the arts and culture from around 70 countries, including 44 official delegations.
Protecting cultural heritage, expanding international humanitarian cooperation, and the impact of new technologies and artificial intelligence on culture and the creative industries are among the themes of this year’s forum.
Upon arriving in St. Petersburg, the minister described culture as one of the main foundations of relations between nations and governments. “Culture is the bedrock and anchor of lasting relations between nations and governments. Government relations may have their ups and downs, but culture provides a point of support, stability, and continuity,” he said.
Referring to Iran-Russia relations, Salehi said, “We have had, and continue to have, good relations with the Russian government and people.” He added that ties between the two countries had strengthened and broadened in recent years, and culture played a significant role in making those relations more enduring, stable, and extensive.
Salehi also described the planning of Iran’s Cultural Week in Russia as one of the most important initiatives for developing cultural ties between the two countries.
He said that various cultural weeks had been held between Iran and Russia over the past two decades. “Last year Iran hosted a 130-member Russian delegation, including the Russian culture minister and artists. This year, Iran’s Cultural Week in Russia will involve more than 120 Iranian artists and production staff,” he noted.
Noting how this year’s program differs from previous editions, Salehi said, “We have not previously held a cultural week of this kind, with such a range of subjects.” He explained that the program would include specialist forums, exhibitions, music performances, and a film week.
He stressed that the events were not limited to staging a handful of cultural programs; strengthening long-term ties between the two countries was also a priority.
As part of the visit, the Iranian culture minister will meet his Russian counterpart in St. Petersburg on Saturday. The two ministers will then convene a meeting of the joint cultural committee.
Before the committee meeting, three working groups—covering culture, the arts, and tourism—will meet with officials from the relevant agencies in both countries. The results of their discussions will be presented at the meeting of the two culture ministers.
Salehi said that the joint committee would exchange and sign various cooperation documents on culture and the arts, including agreements related to cinema.
He also pointed to the wider geographical reach of this year’s Cultural Week as another distinguishing feature. “In the past, cultural-week programs were generally concentrated in the capitals and held in no more than two cities. This year, the event will take place in four cities: Moscow, St. Petersburg, Kazan, and Astrakhan,” he underlined.
According to Salehi, holding events in a wider range of cities will help extend the reach and objectives of Iran’s Cultural Week in Russia.
Another item on Salehi’s itinerary is a gathering with faculty members, students and cultural and intellectual figures at St. Petersburg State University. He will speak about culture’s role in relations and the cultural position of the Islamic Republic of Iran within its civilizational sphere.
After completing the first part of his trip, the culture minister will return to Moscow on Sunday to open the special events marking Iran’s Cultural Week in Russia.
An exhibition of Iranian artists’ visual works will open at Moscow’s Museum of Decorative, Applied, and Folk Arts on Monday. The official opening ceremony for Iran’s Cultural Week in Russia will also take place that day, attended by the culture ministers of both countries.
At the ceremony, Iran’s National Orchestra will perform for an audience of Russian guests.
After Moscow, Iran’s cultural program will continue in Kazan. Iranian visual artists will present their work and hold specialist workshops at the Kazan Kremlin complex, while the Pahlavank troupe will also perform.
A 60-member Iranian music ensemble is scheduled to perform on the evening of Wednesday at an Opera Hall in Kazan.
Fourteen Iranian films will also be screened in Moscow, Kazan, and Astrakhan as part of Iran’s Cultural Week. Kazan will host discussions on the film industry and Iran’s progress in the field.
Next Saturday, October 3, Astrakhan will host a concert featuring Iranian instruments. Film screenings and an exhibition of photographs and posters are also planned there.
Alongside these events, specialist forums will address topics including a commemoration of Nizami Ganjavi, written diplomacy, the potential of the Persian language, and the role of Iranologists in strengthening cultural relations. Iranian and Russian professors of Persian language and literature will also discuss ways to improve Persian-language teaching and preserve the language in Russia.
In another part of his remarks, Salehi referred to Iran’s circumstances following the recent war and described cultural diplomacy as an effective approach to Iran’s engagement with the world. He said Iran could use it to convey its identity, which is marked by epic traditions, to audiences around the world.
Iran previously hosted Russian artists for Russia’s Cultural Days last year, while Iran’s Cultural Week was held in Moscow and St. Petersburg three years ago.
Photo: The Minister of Culture and Islamic Guidance Seyyed Abbas Salehi (L) and the accompanying delegation were welcomed in Moscow by Iran's ambassador to Russia Kazem Jalali (2nd L) on September 24, 2026.
SS/SAB

articles.title: Putin: Moscow was ready for talks with Ukraine after elections, but Kiev attacked polling stations
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow was ready to consider resuming negotiations with Kiev after the elections, but accused Ukraine of attacking Moscow and polling stations.
Speaking to reporters on Friday after the plenary session of the Forum of United Cultures in St. Petersburg, Putin said all proposals for a peaceful settlement were “on the table,” but Russia would “give the matter serious thought” and make decisions based on its own interests.
Putin said Ukrainian attacks had caused casualties and damage to civilian and energy infrastructure, as well as to more than 100 vessels in the Black Sea, including Russian and foreign-flagged ships. He said Russia had repaired the damage.
He said Moscow’s response to the attacks had been severe enough that Kiev was now seeking a halt to strikes, including those targeting energy infrastructure.
Putin also rejected suggestions that Russia was preparing for a war with Europe, saying Moscow had “no such plans” and no reason or motive to escalate tensions.
“We are not preparing for any military action with Europe,” he said. “We have no such plans. And, most importantly, there are no grounds for them.”
‘Aggressive circles’ in Europe
Putin accused what he called “aggressive circles” in Europe of using Ukraine as a tool against Russia and claimed European governments were trying to justify continued support for Kiev by portraying Russia as a threat.
Putin said Russia was aware of what it considers violations of the rights of Russian-speaking populations in the Baltic states but would address the issue through humanitarian and international legal channels.
“We will continue to fight for the rights of our compatriots, but within the framework of international law,” he said.
On US-China relations, Putin welcomed talks between the two countries, saying agreements between the world’s two largest economies would have global economic consequences.
He said Russia’s economic ties with the US were now “almost zero,” while trade with China had reached $240 billion.
Putin said his attendance at the upcoming APEC summit in China had not been finalised and would depend on the situation inside Russia. He said the summit was a significant international event and that he had received an invitation.

articles.title: UN rights chief 'deeply alarmed' by intense fighting in Ethiopia
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
UN rights chief 'deeply alarmed' by escalating fighting in Ethiopia
The United Nations rights chief warned Friday of the threat the escalating fighting in Ethiopia poses to civilians, adding that "deeply troubling" internet and telecommunications interruptions were increasing the risks.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) seized local airports and launched attacks into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara this week with the support of local armed groups, saying they were once again in a "full-blown war" with the federal government.
"I am deeply alarmed by the recent escalation in hostilities... and the harmful impacts it is already having on civilians," said a statement from UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk.
"All parties must urgently de-escalate tensions and avoid a return to full-scale war."
The UN rights office highlighted reports that airstrikes by the Ethiopian National Defence Force (ENDF), some carried out using drones, had hit five Tigray schools on 22 September, resulting in deaths and injuries.
"A mortar strike on 23 September in Kobo town in Amhara reportedly by the ENDF also resulted in civilian deaths," it said.
Turk called on the parties to ensure civilians were protected and to allow "safe and unimpeded humanitarian access to all who need it".
He also criticised the near total disruption of phone networks and the internet, which has raised fears in Tigray of a return to the devastating blockade the northern region experienced during the last civil war.
The 2020-22 conflict was one of the deadliest of recent times, with an estimated death toll of more than 600,000 - when electricity, banking, and almost all aid were cut off.
Turk also deplored an ongoing campaign of "forced mass recruitment of civilians, including children, by TPLF across Tigray", that included reprisal against anyone resisting recruit - and their families.
Turk also mentioned "disturbing reports of arbitrary conscription by government forces".
(AFP)

articles.title: British tourist sparks backlash with Auschwitz cafe rant (VIDEO)
articles.body:
British tourist sparks backlash with Auschwitz cafe rant (VIDEO)
A British tourist has drawn widespread online backlash after a viral TikTok video complaining about drink prices and menu options at a cafe near the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum in Poland, the site of a former Nazi death camp.
At least 1.1 million people were murdered by Nazis at Auschwitz between 1940 and 1945, most of them Jews. Other victims included Poles, Roma and Soviet prisoners of war. Many were murdered in gas chambers, while others died from starvation, disease, brutal forced labor and other forms of persecution. The museum explicitly requires visitors to behave with “due solemnity and respect” while visiting.
However, in a video posted on TikTok on Wednesday and captioned “Prices at Auschwitz,” a woman named Lynne and her daughter made flippant complaints about drinks at a cafe near the memorial.
“Here’s a tip if you’re going to Auschwitz,” Lynne tells followers, pronouncing it like “Oswitch,” before adding: “Take a drink with you. I got a strawberry smoothie which tasted very watered down.” The two then bemoan the lack of decaf and alternative milk and lemonade that tasted “a bit like Dettol,” a toilet cleaner. The pair also complain that the two drinks cost £9 ($12), calling the price “very expensive.”
Always been in two minds about visiting Auschwitz, so I'm glad we're finally cutting through the tourist glitz to get the real info.pic.twitter.com/yV0vd8wkIR
— Hughes-on-the-Wold (@NotThatHughes) September 19, 2026
Lynne has since made her TikTok account private, but the video amassed more than four million views and some 8,000 comments before disappearing from public view at the platform. It also spread across other social media as users seized on the women’s casual focus on refreshments at a site synonymous with mass murder.
Commenters accused the pair of extraordinary “insensitivity,” stressing that Auschwitz is “not a 5 star restaurant experience” or “a theme park,” and saying they should be “ashamed.”
I've ben twice. It's a concentration camp not a fucking theme park. Entry is free. If you feel peckish when viewing the place, u need help. Numb is what you'll feel and Birkenau is the most numbing place.
— Crispy Hoover (@CrispyHoover) September 19, 2026
I’d learn how to pronounce Auschwitz before going there and slagging it off, personally. If they posted this after they’d been in then they are irredeemable pos, because nothing could make 9 quid seem less important. I couldn’t speak for a good hour or 2 afterwards.
— Jacqui (@LancashireLady3) September 19, 2026
How many steps are there between getting your phone out and recording this and then posting it must you go through? At any of which you could stop and questions your actions, then to still just power through and think its fine. Mind boggling.
— finlay (@yalnife) September 19, 2026
They complained about the milk.
The people who died there would have given anything for a sip of water.
Some mocked the women’s complaints.
Hate nothing more than visiting an old concentration camp and the food not being up to scratch !!! pic.twitter.com/WPQ9nqoe8p
— BtotheMtotheC (@BenjaminMcNam10) September 19, 2026
No decaf or milk alternative?! And we thought the inmates had it bad!
— Theophilus.P.Wildebeeste (@Grant_Chapman27) September 19, 2026
I remember when I visited. There is an inscription above the entrance that reads "Arbeit macht frei" which I believe roughly translates as "Lemonade here tastes a bit like Dettol - best avoided"
— BigBridesmaid (@BigBridesmaid) September 19, 2026
Others suggested the video was simply designed to provoke reactions – invoking the idea that bad publicity is still publicity – but still slammed the decision to use a place associated with mass murder as the backdrop for something so “crass and inane.”
In follow-up videos, Lynne lashed out at critics as “wokes,” appearing to miss the point of the backlash while shifting blame toward the museum. She insisted the cafe was separate from the memorial – “No-one died there. No-one was gassed there” – before questioning why refreshments were sold at all and accusing the site of becoming a “money-making scheme.”
A spokesman for the museum told The Times that the cafe is outside the visitor services center, independently operated, and displays its prices clearly.
“The essential point remains that people come to the Auschwitz Memorial to learn about the history of the German Nazi concentration and extermination camp, to confront the fate of its victims and to commemorate them,” the spokesman argued.
The museum repeatedly reminds visitors that Auschwitz is a memorial rather than a conventional tourist attraction, urging them to behave with respect and to avoid conduct that undermines the memory of its victims.
Still, it has faced controversies over visitors and businesses treating the site in ways critics regard as inappropriate. In 2020, a TikTok trend drew condemnation after users role-played as Holocaust victims. A year later, TripAdvisor removed an offensive review of Auschwitz after initially saying it complied with its guidelines. In 2023, an “Ice Love” ice-cream stand installed near the camp prompted another outcry.
Russian officials, meanwhile, have repeatedly accused Western countries of distorting the history of World War II, including diminishing the Soviet Union’s role in defeating Nazi Germany. Moscow has pointed to the dismantling of Soviet war memorials in Eastern Europe and the honoring of historical Nazi collaborators in Ukraine as examples of what it describes as attempts to “rewrite history.”
Last month, Moscow condemned plans for a supermarket and logistics facility at the site of the former Hirtenberg women’s concentration camp in Austria, accusing Vienna of erasing the memory of its victims. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described the planned development as an attempt to effectively “pave over” that memory.

articles.title: Iraq seeks exemption from US ban on Iran airlines
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq seeks exemption from US ban on Iran airlines
The Iraqi government said Saturday it was holding talks with the United States to secure an exemption from the ban on Iranian airlines, which has disrupted travel for patients, students and pilgrims.
All Iraqi airports enforced the ban this week, resulting in major disruption at the airport of the holy city of Najaf, the main destination for Iranian flights to Iraq.
"The Iraqi government is holding direct talks with the American side to exempt certain Iraqi airports from these measures," the prime minister's media office said.
An exemption would allow flights to resume "for humanitarian reasons, including medical treatment, education, religious visits, and for the interest of civilians," it added.
Iranian airlines mainly carry Iraqi Shia pilgrims to Iran's holy cities or Iranians visiting sacred sites in Iraq. The flights also serve Iraqi students studying in Iran and patients seeking medical treatment there.
Several Iraqis have said that enforcing the US sanctions has left them scrambling for solutions, with some fearing they would lose access to treatment in Iran or others stranded there with little choice but to take the more than 12-hour journey home by land.
Iraq has joined several countries including the United Arab Emirates in enforcing the US ban, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Iranian airlines would be "shut down" on Wednesday.
Relations between between Iraq and neighbouring Iran, both Shia-majority countries, have long been close, due to religious kinship as well as political and economic interests.
Iraqi airlines stopped flying to Iran at the start of the Middle East war in February.

articles.title: How online toxicity silences the majority and fuels power users
articles.body:
In online political discussions, a small fraction of highly active users typically generates the vast majority of content while most people silently observe. A recent experiment reveals that polite and constructive environments encourage silent readers to post their first comment, but the most active users are driven to post more when discussions become toxic. These findings were published in the journal Science Advances.
Online spaces are central to modern political discourse, yet they suffer from a stark participation divide. A vocal minority often dominates the conversation, creating a distorted picture of public opinion. Researchers refer to these highly active individuals as power users, while the vast majority who consume content without posting are known as lurkers.
This uneven participation raises concerns about a spiral of silence. This is a theory where citizens withhold their views if they believe those views are unpopular. In the modern attention economy of social media, extreme or hostile content often gains the most visibility.
If only a specific type of user feels comfortable producing this content, online discussions may look much more polarized than the actual public. A cycle emerges where moderate voices retreat, leaving the platform to those who thrive on conflict.
To understand what drives people into these distinct roles, researchers need to observe communities as they form. Lead author Lisa Oswald, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, alongside colleagues William Small Schulz and Philipp Lorenz-Spreen, designed a study to track exactly how users select into active or silent roles. They also wanted to test whether financial rewards or strict civility rules could level the playing field.
The researchers recruited 520 participants from the United States through advertisements on the social media platform Reddit. After participants completed an initial survey about their political views and online habits, they were randomly assigned to one of six private Reddit communities created specifically for the study.
Over four weeks, the research team prompted the groups with 20 different political issues. They asked participants to discuss topics ranging from immigration and gun control to universal basic income and artificial intelligence.
To test ways to close the participation gap, the researchers applied different conditions to the communities. Two communities served as a control group with standard platform settings. In two other communities, participants received a financial incentive, earning two dollars for every day they wrote a substantive comment.
The final two communities operated under a moderation condition. In these groups, users received frequent reminders to stay civil and respectful alongside automated spam filters.
Participants completed weekly surveys about their experiences and perceptions of the group dynamics. The researchers then categorized the users into two groups. One group consisted of those who never commented, while the other included those who wrote at least one comment.
For the active users, the team tracked the total number of comments they contributed. The results revealed a mirrored psychological mechanism driving both initial participation and heavy posting.
Participants who remained silent were more likely to view the group as polarized and toxic. These users indicated they preferred environments that felt respectful, knowledgeable, and constructive. If a community felt hostile, they chose to simply read the posts and say nothing.
For users who crossed the threshold to write at least one comment, the exact opposite held true. The active users posted more frequently when they perceived the group as polarized, toxic, and lacking in knowledge.
The researchers noted that an abrasive environment suppresses the voices of the silent majority. At the same time, it acts as a catalyst for a less sensitive minority to dominate the conversation. The objective toxicity of the group interacts with a user’s personal sensitivity to hostility to determine their behavior.
The interventions designed to improve the conversation had mixed results. Financial incentives did encourage more people to speak up, narrowing the participation gap between lurkers and power users. Providing a direct reward successfully motivated hesitant users to join the conversation.
The moderation condition failed to change participation levels or improve the quality of the discourse. Reminding users to remain civil did not reduce the participation gap, nor did it lower the toxicity of the comments. The researchers observed that simply asking for polite behavior is unlikely to change the underlying dynamics of online engagement.
The researchers also analyzed how social feedback influenced user behavior. They found that receiving positive votes on comments was associated with increased posting the following day. When participants received negative feedback through downvotes, they were less likely to continue participating.
The experiment also tracked whether engaging in these political discussions changed participants’ minds. Over the four weeks, the research team found no statistically significant differences in political attitude changes between the treatment groups and the control group. Measures of political trust and polarization remained relatively stable regardless of the community rules or incentives.
Descriptively across all groups, participants reported lower levels of political interest and issue knowledge by the end of the study. The researchers suggested this might be due to an intimidation effect. The comments posted during the study were considerably longer and more detailed than typical Reddit posts, which may have led some participants to feel they could not add anything to the conversation.
The study took place in a uniquely controlled environment that differs from organic social media use. The participants were predominantly liberal, meaning the discussions lacked the deep ideological clashes often found in broader public forums. Additionally, the overall toxicity of the comments during the experiment was exceptionally low from the start.
This low baseline of toxicity left little room for the moderation treatment to make a measurable impact. Future research could explore whether strictly enforced rules, such as banning hostile users rather than just reminding them to be civil, might yield different outcomes. Scientists also plan to investigate how these group dynamics function on other platforms with different community structures and algorithms.
The study, “Disentangling participation in online political discussions with a collective field experiment,” was authored by Lisa Oswald, William Small Schulz, and Philipp Lorenz-Spreen.

articles.title: Artificial
articles.body:
Artificial
« previous post |
From Donald Trump's recent UN speech:
The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now, hereinafter officially called Super Intelligence, changing the name, and that the use of the word "artificial" makes intelligence fake. It makes it sound fake. And it is not fake. It's actually amazing, but we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports.
From this point forward, all of United States documents and, hopefully the world's will be changed to use the much more accurate term "super" as opposed to "artificial". So it's Super Intelligence. In other words, welcome to the new world of Super Intelligence-SI. SI, let's see if that goes, it sounds much better. It is much better, and it's much more accurate. Let's see if I have any power. Maybe I do, and maybe I don't. We're going to find out pretty soon.
This reminds me of one of my favorite examples of semantic drift.
The OED's sense I.1.a. for artificial, dating to c1425, is "Of a thing: made or constructed by human skill, esp. in imitation of, or as a substitute for, something which is made or occurs naturally; man-made."
Scrolling down through other senses over the years, we get some negatively-evaluated senses, like 1.4.a "Contrived or fabricated for a particular purpose, esp. for deception; resulting from artifice; feigned, fictitious", as well as some positively-evaluated (or at least neutral) ones, like II.6 "According to the principles of an art or science; scientific, systematic."
But then there's II.9.a "Of a thing: skilfully made or contrived; cleverly constructed", flagged as Obsolete, with citations through 1833, for example these (quotations expanded from the original sources):
1663 How to make a brazen or stone head, in the midst of a great field or garden, so artificial and natural, that though a man speak never so softly, and even whispers into the ear thereof, it will presently open its mouth, and resolve the question in French, Latin, Welsh, Irish, or English, in good terms, uttering it out of his mouth, and then shut it until the next question be asked.
1738  The artificial and elegant Structure of the Eyes, and the great fitness of their Parts, for the offices of Vision, are illustrated by the Laws of Opticks.
1833  The collocation of the words is so artificial in Shakspeare and Milton that you may as well think of pushing a brick out of that wall with your finger as of displacing a word without injury from one of their sentences.
The 1633 example is from The Century of Inventions of the Marquis of Worcester, originally (?) published in 1825. The cited passage continues:
Albertus Magnus, a celebrated philosopher of the thirteenth century, is said to have constructed an automaton which not only performed all the apparent motions of life, but absolutely answered questions. It is recorded of Thomas Aquinas, that, having accidentally seen the head, he was so terrified that he broke it in pieces, upon which Albert exclaimed: Periit opus triginta annorum! Though this appears one of the earliest instances of a speaking automaton constructed by one of the laity, there is no doubt but that the method of conveying answers to various interrogatories, by the agency of concealed pipes or a speaking trumpet, was practised at a very early period. That the impostor Alexander, however, caused his Æsculapius to speak in this manner is expressly related by Lucan. He took, says this author, instead of a pipe, the gullet of a crane, and transmitted the voice through it to the mouth of the statue. But the invention of the invisible girl, which may be considered as an improvement on the oracular responses of the darker ages, infinitely surpassed any of those hitherto recorded.
This very ingenious apparatus was publicly exhibited both at Bristol and in London for a considerable period, during which time no discovery was made of its internal mechanism; and it is probable that its construction would have remained a secret to all but the exhibitors, but for the ingenuity of Mr. (now Professor) Millington, who, in a course of Lectures delivered in the winter of 1806, explained the manner in which it was performed.
The visible part of the apparatus connected with the invisible girl was thus constructed: first a mahogany frame resembling a bedstead, having at the corners four upright posts about five feet high, was united by a cross-rail near the top, and two or more cross-rails near the bottom, to strengthen the frame, which was about four feet square. The frame thus constructed was placed upon the floor, and to the top of each of the four pillars were attached as many strong bent brass wires converging towards the top, where they were secured by a crown and other ornaments. From these wires a hollow copper ball was suspended by slight ribbons, so as to cut off all possible communication with the frame. The globe thus supported was supposed to contain the invisible being, as the voice apparently proceeded from the interior of it: and for this purpose, it was equipped with four trumpets, placed round it in a horizontal direction, and at right angles to each other; the trumpet mouths coming to within about half an inch of the respective cross-rails of the frame surrounding them.
When a question was proposed, it was asked from any side of the frame, and spoken into one of the trumpets, and an answer immediately proceeded from the whole of them, so loud as to be distinctly heard by the inquirer, and yet so distant and feeble, that it appeared as if coming from a very diminutive being. In this the whole of the artifice consisted; and the variations were so contrived that the answer might be returned in several languages, a kiss might be returned, the breath producing the voice was felt, and songs were sung, accompanied by the piano-forte, &c. To produce this illusion, the sound was conveyed by a tube, in a manner similar to the old and well known contrivance of the speaking bust; the invisible girl only differing in one circumstance; that an artificial echo was produced by means of the trumpets and hollow globe, in consequence of which the sound was completely reversed.
In the invisible girl the orifice of the tube was in one of the handrails just opposite the mouth of one of the trumpets, the opening being concealed by reeds and other mouldings; the tube itself, which was about half an inch in diameter, ran through half the handrail, then down one of the corner posts, and from thence under the floor till it reached a large deal case almost similar to an inverted funnel, along the side of which it rose till it came nearly into contact with the ear of the confederate, who with a piano-forte, &c. was concealed in this case. Any question asked by a voice directed into one of the trumpets was immediately reflected back from the concave interior surface of the globe to the orifice of the tube, along which it was conveyed so as to be distinctly heard by the person in the deal case, who returned the requisite answer, which appeared to come precisely from the interior of the globe. A small hole closed with glass was likewise left through the deal case and side wall of the apartment, by means of which the concealed person had an opportunity of observing and commenting upon any circumstance which occurred in the room.
Unquestionably very artificial and natural!

articles.title: Insecurity in Hormuz result of "US breach of its commitments"
articles.body:
Iran’s top diplomat made the remarks in a meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in New York on Friday on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly (UNGA).
During this meeting, the two top diplomats exchanged their views on host of issues, including bilateral relation in various sectors, including political, economic, trade, transport, and energy fields and also coordination within the international organizations.
Araghchi commended Russia's responsible stance in opposing the US's belligerent unilateralism and the misuse of international organizations to exert pressure on the independent nations.
The foreign ministers of Iran and Russia also exchanged views on developments in the West Asia region following the United States' repeated reneging on its commitments and its violation of the terms and conditions of the Islamabad understanding.
Araghchi briefed his Russian counterpart on the latest status of negotiations and the understanding reached between Iran and Oman regarding the establishment of a safe shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as the ongoing efforts of mediators to convey the necessary conditions for a return to the diplomatic process.
The current insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz is the direct result of the United States' breach of its commitments and criminal actions against Iran, he said, recalling Iran's good faith during the negotiations that led to the agreement ending the war.
The Iranian foreign minister emphasized that the Islamic Republic of Iran—just as it demonstrated seriousness in the diplomatic arena—remains determined to defend its national interests and security and to prevent the US from exploiting the Strait of Hormuz to threaten Iran's national security.
Reiterating Russia's principled stance condemning the military aggression by the US and Israel against Iran—as well as the attempts by the US and its allies to instrumentalize international organizations to advance their own agendas, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov emphasized the importance of all nations adhering to international law and the principles of the UN Charter.
